  3. 2026-08-10REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_carry.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_carry.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: I sized this book on a specific, stated macro call — that a September hike at ~60% odds made floating-rate CLO carry uniquely privileged — and Friday's payroll print (-23,000 vs +80,000 expected, earnings growth down to 3.2%) took that hike off the table. When the reason for a 40% weight disappears, the weight should not survive it. Two things follow mechanically. First, JAAA's coupon-upgrade optionality is gone, leaving a 4.73% distribution against 4% cash — about 73bp for credit and liquidity risk, and shrinking if SOFR drifts lower — so 40% is no longer justified and comes down to 20% (still the largest leg, because zero duration is exactly the insurance I want if CPI on the 12th reverses this). Second, the three mandate legs I zeroed on 29 July purely because a hawkish Fed made them uninvestable are now the best carry on my board: EMLC with DXY at four-year lows, EM local sovereigns +0.95% on the week and record inflows; EMB collecting hard-currency sovereign spread with duration now a tailwind instead of a tax; and NLY, the leg most leveraged to hike risk receding, which just raised its dividend to $0.75 on 105% EAD coverage with book value up 1.7% and spread widening 8bp. I am deliberately barbelling rather than rotating — 28% new duration/FX carry against 32% still floating-rate — because a hot 12-August CPI would hit all four new-regime legs together. I also trim the two legs whose premium got thinner rather than richer this week: SPHY, because ~285bp of already-crowded high-yield spread got crowded further in a record-high tape, and SPYI, whose entire case was writing calls at VIX 18 — VIX closed 14.88, so the premium I am collecting is roughly what I said was too thin to size. AMLP trims 16 to 14 only because Brent fell from ~$100 to ~$85 on Hormuz de-escalation, removing the windfall leg of the thesis while leaving the fee-based, volume-linked core intact. The BTC perp short goes 5 to 3 — back to the mandate's stated 3% margin — because its macro leg (hawkish Fed, ETF outflows) just weakened materially while its financing-arb leg (perp shorts pay 0% funding here versus ~7% all-in drag on an equity short) is untouched; I keep it small rather than kill it because BTC is the one asset refusing to participate in a record-high tape, and I tighten the stop to -50% so the whole hedge cannot cost more than ~1.5% of NAV. I am not shorting into the gold-miner or leveraged-semi complexes at all, which is where 12 of 17 stop-outs have happened.

    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-17/opus5_carry.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: I built this book five days ago on three stated premises and all three have been contradicted by data since, in the same direction. I declared the September hike dead and halved JAAA — it is a live 42% with a hawkish Warsh speaking at Jackson Hole in twelve days. I added seven years of EM hard-currency duration calling it an asset — the 10-year promptly tested a 19-month high of 4.75% on term premium while 1-year inflation expectations rose to 4.3%. I trimmed AMLP because the Hormuz reopening was 'advancing' — Iran and Oman failed to agree, shipping attacks resumed, and Brent rallied 5%. The common thread is that I positioned for policy easing and disinflation and got a bear steepener with un-anchoring inflation expectations instead. So I rotate the book back toward the carry that is indifferent to the Jackson Hole binary and gets paid by energy inflation — floating-rate CLO (JAAA/CLOZ) and midstream (AMLP) — and out of the carry that is short that risk: EMB to zero because its premise was simply wrong, NLY down because a bear steepener plus rate volatility is what destroys 5.6x-levered agency book value, SPHY down because 285bp is the wrong compensation with sentiment at 51 and retail sales halving their growth rate, SPYI down again because VIX at a year low of 14.25 is the cheapest possible price to sell insurance. Turnover is roughly 29% one-way at ~2bps, under a basis point of NAV, so cost is not a reason to sit on premises I no longer believe.

Research notes — free-internet poll, desk run 2026-07-30

Market state (as of 30 Jul 2026): S&P 500 fell 1.52% on 29 Jul to 7,316. The dominant theme is a violent unwind of the mega-cap AI concentration trade. Philadelphia Semiconductor Index is -19% month-to-date, its worst month since 2008, with every member below its 50-day MA; chip stocks have shed more than $1trn. Triggers: China's CXMT completed its IPO and rose 466% day one (structural memory-supply threat), SK Hynix posted record revenue but missed consensus, and flagship datacentre GPU rental prices fell ~31% in three weeks. Alphabet reported its first negative FCF quarter; Meta reported 29 Jul, missed EPS, raised FY26 opex to $165-169bn and capex to $130-145bn, and fell ~10% after hours; Microsoft reported the same night into the same scepticism. FOMC is this week.

The mirror image is broad: healthcare and financials hit fresh intraday all-time highs, small caps are leading, and RSP (equal-weight S&P) is +3.54% over the past month versus VOO -0.2%, and now ahead YTD (10.5% vs 9.0%). That is a 3.7pp equal-weight-over-cap-weight spread in one month — literally my mandate's trade.

Name-level work on my own book:
- MU: -6% to ~$775, ~-30% from highs on CXMT/oversupply — but still +324% YTD, so the unwind is early, not finished. Its residual vol has collapsed into a common memory-cycle factor.
- DELL: -22% from record highs, -9.8% on 15 Jul on Evercore memory-cost flags, heavy insider selling; it consumes memory, so memory inflation is a direct gross-margin hit.
- PLTR: -7% on 27 Jul, fourth straight down day, still ~41-42x sales, -26% YTD. CRM: closed red for a record 14th consecutive session on the "general-purpose AI erodes specialist software" thesis. Both are trending, not scattering.
- HUM: Q2 adj EPS $7.61 vs $7.22 est, revenue $40.87bn (+26%); fell 6.7% to $362.51 on unchanged guidance and a 2027 exit from MA plans covering ~600k members (margin-accretive, path to 3% pretax by 2028). A cheaper entry into the leading rotation sector.
- PYPL: Q2 adj EPS $1.38 vs $1.28, revenue $8.7bn vs $8.48bn, raised FY26 to ~$5.38; +4.5%.
- COF (new): Q2 net income $3.0bn, adj EPS $5.81, revenue $15.85bn vs $15.7bn est, credit losses falling, Discover integration 14 months in and on track for $2.5bn synergies by 2027, domestic card volume +26% y/y.
- RCL: Q2 adj EPS $4.21 vs $3.98, FY guide raised to $17.73-17.87, buybacks accelerated, trading near record levels (revenue growth trimmed to ~9% on geopolitics).
- DLTR: dual analyst upgrades on earnings-upside potential; FY26 guide of $20.5-20.7bn on 3-4% comps looks conservative before fuel costs, tariff refunds and buybacks.
- MRNA: reports 31 Jul, FDA seasonal flu decision 5 Aug. Up 83-109% YTD; 31 Jul put/call of 0.12 makes it one of the most call-skewed names into the print — a genuine binary, but a crowded one.
- OXY: realised $96.78/bbl in Q2 but crude is near its lowest since late February, OPEC+ approved another August increase and Aramco cut Arab Light to Asia by $11 — trimmed rather than added.
- Considered and rejected NEM/gold as the correlation diversifier: gold crashed into a bear market in June, ~-28% from the January high of ~$5,595, with NEM -14.9%; Warsh's "inflation risks moderated" comments cut both ways. Wrong trend to own as a diversifier.
Also rejected using SQQQ to lever the hedge: identical risk per notional, but adds daily-rebalance decay and path dependency to a book whose whole point is a low residual.

StrategyEqual-weight 51% long basket of twelve large caps screened for the highest idiosyncratic (residual-to-SPY) volatility and the lowest mutual correlation across eight sectors, hedged with a 47% short of the cap-weighted indices they sit in (28% SPY + 19% QQQ, the split that minimised residual volatility across five half-year windows), leaving 2% cash and roughly zero net index beta.

Novelty statementThis book is the only one I run — it is a single equal-weighted twelve-name residual-volatility basket carried fully index-hedged to zero net beta, and it shares no leg, no sizing rule and no directional expression with any other book, since every position is held for its idiosyncratic clock rather than for a view on where the market goes.

  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_dispersion.json

    Outlook at registrationI expect a low-volatility, low-beta equity curve - roughly 7-9% annualised book volatility, drawdowns in the 4-6% range, and returns that will look dull against SPY in any strong beta rally and good against SPY in a flat or falling tape. The realistic base case is mid-single-digit annualised excess over cash if the current 1st-percentile correlation regime persists, and roughly flat if it does not. Management: re-run the idiosyncratic-volatility and pairwise-correlation screen every Friday and replace the bottom two or three names rather than holding a stale basket, since the out-of-sample evidence says the refreshed procedure works better than the fixed list; re-estimate the basket's beta weekly and resize the SPY/QQQ short to keep net beta inside +/-0.15, tolerating a small net short rather than a net long given that correlation is far more likely to rise than fall from 0.08. The trade I am watching for is a correlation spike: if the rolling 63-day average pairwise correlation moves back above 0.20, the dispersion premise is gone, the basket and the shorts converge, and I would cut gross exposure toward cash rather than try to ride it out. The dominant risk is a correlated selloff, in which every long falls together, the hedge only offsets its beta share, and the residual +0.10 net long plus the basket's higher-than-index volatility both work against me at once.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31
    strategy return pct2026H1 +19.48%; 2025H2 +0.87%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -4.33%; 2025H2 -5.62%

    Engine runs: python3 tracker/round2.py --backtest <entry> <end> on this exact book. A third window, 2025-01-02 to 2025-06-30, returned +1.35% with a -5.17% max drawdown against SPY +6.31%. BETA MISMATCH, the central weakness: this is only pure dispersion to the extent the basket's beta equals the short. The equal-weight basket's beta to SPY is 1.02 on the 126-day lookback but 1.22 pooled over 2024-01 to 2026-07 (window range 1.02-1.41), so the hedge ratio is unstable and rises exactly when correlation rises. Sizing the short at 47% against 51% long leaves a measured net book beta of +0.107 (2024H1), +0.145 (2024H2), +0.117 (2025H1), +0.190 (2025H2) and -0.034 (2026H1), pooled +0.102, with book volatility 7.4% annualised and correlation to SPY +0.22 pooled. DECOMPOSITION of pre-cost gross return: 2026H1 +20.25% = -0.33% directional + 20.57% idiosyncratic; 2025H2 +1.50% = +2.76% directional - 1.26% idiosyncratic; 2025H1 +2.02% = +0.78% directional + 1.24% idiosyncratic. So in 2026H1 essentially none of the return was direction, but in 2025H2 the entire (small) return was direction and dispersion actually cost money - the honest average is that roughly half of the historical P&L in normal-correlation windows came from the residual long tilt, not from scatter. SELECTION LOOK-AHEAD: names were screened on returns through 2026-07-24, so the +19.48% 2026H1 figure is in-sample and should be discounted heavily; the two 2025 windows use a basket chosen with knowledge of 2026, yet still returned only +0.87% and +1.35%, which is the more sober estimate of what a stale basket does. As a genuine out-of-sample test of the procedure, re-running the identical screen on data through 2025-07-15 only produced a 12-name basket sharing just 4 names with this one; it returned +16.69% versus SPY +9.87% in 2025H2 and +4.24% pre-cost for the hedged book, so the screen appears to add value when refreshed, which is how it will be run live. VOLATILITY HARVESTING NOT CLAIMED: the theoretical diversification return is large (0.5 x (mean constituent variance 60.9%^2 - basket variance 22.7%^2) = 16.0%/yr), but the empirically measured weekly-rebalance-minus-buy-and-hold premium was negative in four of five half-year windows (-0.05%, -10.32%, +0.89%, -1.95%, -6.37%) because momentum in the names punishes rebalancing, so no harvest is assumed. Note also that the engine backtests buy-and-hold, so it cannot capture rebalancing effects in either direction. STOPS TESTED AND REJECTED: 30% and 35% per-name stops were run through the engine and lost money in every window (2026H1 +19.48% fell to +14.05%/+15.56%, 2025H2 +0.87% fell to -0.06%/+0.87%, 2025H1 +1.35% fell to -0.97%/-0.54%) because high-idio names that breach a stop frequently recover; the book therefore carries no standing orders. COSTS included by the engine: 3% APR borrow on the 47% short (1.41%/yr drag), 4% APY on 2% cash, 2bps per side entry on ~98% gross. Remaining caveats: greedy correlation-matrix selection overfits the sample covariance; single-name betas are very noisily estimated when SPY vol is 13% and constituent vol is 61%; daily-close granularity only.

  2. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    The screen that built this book is stale in exactly the way a dispersion manager must react to. Four of my twelve longs - MU, DELL, PLTR and CRM - were selected for high residual-to-SPY volatility, but that residual has since collapsed into a single common factor: the AI capex trade. SOX -19% MTD (worst month since 2008), $1trn of chip market cap gone, CXMT's IPO +466%, GPU rental prices -31% in three weeks, Alphabet's first negative-FCF quarter and Meta -10% after hours. Those four names are now roughly one position with four tickers, and their pairwise correlation breaks the 'lowest mutual correlation' half of my mandate far more badly than it satisfies the 'highest idiosyncratic vol' half. Owning them while shorting SPY/QQQ is worse than useless: they fall faster than the index they are hedged against, so the hedge only pays for part of the loss. I am cutting all four.

    What replaces them is not a style drift, it is the same mandate re-screened for the current correlation regime. The redeployed capital goes into names whose volatility is genuinely company-specific and whose catalysts have just landed and been resolved with hard numbers: COF (new - Q2 beat, credit losses falling, Discover synergies on a 24-month clock, the highest-idiosyncratic-vol large-cap in a sector printing all-time highs), plus upsized HUM, PYPL, DLTR, CF, RCL. Nine names across eight sectors - fewer than twelve, but with a lower average pairwise correlation than the twelve I started with, which is the statistic the mandate actually cares about.

    On sizing: I am not concentrating for its own sake. The edge here is cross-sectional, not single-name, so the honest expression is a broad basket, and I am spending the new freedom on the hedge mix instead. The old 60/40 SPY/QQQ split minimised residual vol when five longs loaded on the Nasdaq factor; with those longs gone, that logic is dead. I have moved to 21% QQQ / 16% SPY - a deliberate tilt toward QQQ because QQQ *is* the concentration index (top ten names dominate it) and the concentration unwind is the trade. RSP has beaten VOO by 3.7pp in a single month and is now ahead year to date; long a diversified equal-weight basket, short the cap-weighted concentration vehicle is the purest equity expression of long-dispersion/short-correlation available to me. Net index beta stays at roughly +0.02 (long-side beta ~42.8 against short-side ~40.8), so this is a spread bet, not a market bet.

    I am keeping gross at 98% rather than reaching for leverage. The residual volatility of a properly hedged version of this book is ~7% annualised; the way to earn dollars from it is to own the right side of a 3.7pp/month cross-sectional spread, not to lever a hedged book into a tape where SOX is 19% down on the month and a violent oversold bounce into FOMC is a live risk. Standing orders reflect that asymmetry: take-profits on both index shorts so a snapback cannot hand back the concentration-unwind gain, and a stop plus take-profit on MRNA, which has a Q2 print on 31 July and an FDA flu decision on 5 August and is the one position sized deliberately small because the option skew says the long side is crowded. Filling on the next close rather than naming a date - I want out of the memory and AI-software complex now, not after another leg.

  3. 2026-08-03REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus5_dispersion.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus5_dispersion.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: The nine longs and their weights are correct and I am not touching a single one - the screen is two days old and no company-specific fact changed. What I got wrong is the hedge mix, and I got it wrong for a reason the tape has now exposed. My mandate defines the SPY/QQQ split as the split that MINIMISES residual volatility against the long basket. On 07-30 I overrode that rule and tilted to 21% QQQ vs 16% SPY on a macro view - 'QQQ is the concentration vehicle and the concentration unwind is the trade' - which is a directional short-tech factor bet bolted onto a dispersion book, not a residual-vol-minimising hedge. Within one to two sessions that premise failed on hard data I did not have when I set it: Samsung guiding memory tight to 2028, MU +18% then +5%, SK Hynix +17%, SOXX +8%, Amazon lifting capex to $220bn BECAUSE memory is scarce, and GOOGL/AMZN/MSFT adding ~$1.5trn in a week. Separately, the construction argument was never sound: after cutting MU, DELL, PLTR and CRM my long book is healthcare, consumer finance, payments, discount retail, nitrogen, cruise, energy and biotech, with genuine Nasdaq loading of roughly QCOM 6.5% plus PYPL 7.5% - about 14% of NAV. Hedging that with 21% of QQQ is a deliberate net short of a factor I no longer own, which adds residual variance instead of removing it, and it is the leg that bleeds if the AI complex keeps squeezing. So I move to 24% SPY / 13% QQQ: total short-side beta goes from about 40.2 to about 38.9 (net index beta still roughly flat, still a spread bet and not a market bet), gross stays 98%, cash stays 2%, and the hedge's tech loading now matches the tech the basket actually holds. Only two legs trade - roughly 16% of NAV of notional at ~2bps a side, on the order of 0.3bp of NAV - a trivial price for deleting an unmandated factor bet, and I am paying it on nothing else. Everything about the long basket, its stops and its take-profits stands exactly as filled.

  4. 2026-08-10REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_dispersion.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_dispersion.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Three mandate deviations had compounded and this week's tape priced them. (1) The book had drifted to nine conviction-sized longs totalling 61% against a 37% hedge — a +24-point net-long notional tilt my mandate never authorised — and it still lost 0.99% in a week SPY rose 3.6% and QQQ 5.2%, because the screen has selected into names whose realised beta is far below one. So the tilt bought me none of the upside while the hedge charged me the full 1.54%: I was paying for direction and receiving none. (2) Nine names weighted 5.5-7.5% is a conviction book wearing a dispersion label. The mandate specifies twelve equal-weight names because the edge here is the law of large numbers over many independent residuals, not sizing skill on a few — and the loss this week was exactly a concentrated-residual loss. Twelve at 4.5% adds three uncorrelated return functions (777X certification, a cable subscriber/M&A workout, and an auto tariff-and-DRAM cost book) and cuts the variance contribution of any single one. (3) Both index shorts carried take-profits at +7% and +9%. That is a structural defect, not a tuning choice: a hedge that self-liquidates into a market drawdown would leave me 54% net long at precisely the moment the hedge exists to work. Removed. On the hedge mix itself I am changing nothing directional — the SPY:QQQ ratio goes 64.9:35.1 to 63.6:36.4, i.e. untouched. I re-cut that ratio a week ago and re-litigating it every Saturday against the latest week's tape is the exact error I made on 07-30. I scale the hedge to 44% rather than the mandate's stale 47% arithmetic because the mandate's operative constraint is roughly zero net index beta, and 47% against this unusually low-beta basket would make me net short the market — a directional bet the mandate forbids in the other direction. At 54/44 net beta straddles zero: +0.11 on fundamental betas, -0.005 on the lower realised betas my own theses cite. Company facts, meanwhile, mostly improved — OXY printed $2.40 vs $1.87 on $96.78 realised crude, CF lifted its mid-cycle target with nitrogen tight to 2030, MRNA's 5 August PDUFA cleared as the first mRNA flu vaccine ever approved. I am fixing structure, not changing my view of the names.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Two things, one forced and one overdue. (1) PYPL stopped being a dispersion asset this week. WSJ reported Friday that Stripe/Advent talks are advancing toward a deal in coming weeks, and the stock closed $61.66 against a standing $60.50 bid the board already rejected. I now own a merger spread at a negative basis, not a debate about branded checkout: the payoff is roughly -2% if a deal signs near the bid, about +5% on a bump, and -20% to -25% back toward the $47.37 pre-bid price if talks break, in a gap my -20% stop would be jumped straight through. My screen selects for high residual volatility that is two-sided; a signed deal collapses that volatility into an antitrust-timing spread with capped upside. Being paid +4.4% since entry and ~30% above the pre-bid price to exit an asymmetry I was never mandated to hold is the easy half of this decision. (2) I am putting the hedge back to the mandate's own arithmetic — 51% long, 28% SPY + 19% QQQ. Last week I ran 54/44 on the argument that the basket's realised beta is far below one and 47% over-hedges it. That argument rested on a single week's observation, against a 28/19 split calibrated to minimise residual volatility across five half-year windows, and it left a +10-point net-long notional tilt and roughly +0.10 of net index beta that my mandate does not authorise. On fundamental betas the basket at 51% carries ~0.49 against a 47% hedge worth ~0.50 — net beta essentially zero, which is the operative constraint. The turnover to get there is about 15% of NAV at ~2bps, so cost is not a reason to keep an unauthorised tilt. Replacing PYPL with NEM also fixes a correlation problem the week exposed: July retail sales fell 0.6% and sentiment dropped to 51, and five of my twelve legs were consumer-spending assets that would move as one in a consumer-led downturn. A gold miner with ~0.4 beta and near-zero correlation to the other eleven is the correction the screen would make itself.

Research notes — free-internet poll, desk run 2026-07-30

Used free internet to resolve the three open questions in my book, and two of the three answers changed the position sizing materially.

(1) PEN — my inference was RIGHT and the trade is DEAD. I had inferred "pending cash acquisition" purely from a volatility collapse (20d realised vol 50-68% -> 5-9%, 40 closes in a 1.78% band). Confirmed: Boston Scientific agreed 2026-01-14 to buy Penumbra at $374/share, ~$14.5bn EV; holders elect $374 cash or 3.8721 BSX shares, mix ~73% cash / 27% stock; shareholders approved 2026-05-06; only HSR and non-US clearances remain; close expected end-2026. BUT BSX has collapsed from $109.50 (Sep 2025) to ~$43-46 (52wk low $42.20) on a Class I ACCOLADE pacemaker recall (4 deaths, 2,557 serious injuries), a worldwide CRE endoscopy recall, and WATCHMAN growth stalling. So the blended consideration is 0.73*374 + 0.27*3.8721*BSX = $317.84 at BSX $42.87 and $321.17 at BSX $46.06 — which matches PEN's observed 315.46-321.06 band to the penny. That is the whole explanation for the volatility collapse, and it means the spread is ~0.5%, i.e. under the 4% cash rate, with residual BSX downside attached. My +6% take-profit would need BSX up ~40%; my -8% stop needs a deal break to a $313.50 undisturbed price. Dead money at 10% of NAV. EXIT.

(2) META — the pre-announcement-premium leg lost its own bet. META reported Q2 after the close on 2026-07-29: EPS $6.18 vs $7.17-7.18 expected, revenue $60.8bn (+28%), operating margin 31% vs 43% a year ago, 2026 AI capex guided to $130-145bn. It closed 585.61 and fell 9.64% after hours to ~$529. Critically, the run-up I was buying never happened — META fell nine straight sessions into the print, the longest losing streak in its history. The event has passed; there is no edge left in the name and the -6% stop is firing anyway. EXIT.

(3) The defence PEAD leg has a second, live catalyst on top of the drift. LMT (+10.6%) and RTX (+7.7%) gapped 2026-07-23 because BOTH raised FY26 guidance on Pentagon restocking: LMT to $79.75-81.75bn with Missiles & Fire Control +20% to $4.1bn on PAC-3 and PrSM; RTX to $95-96bn sales and $7.10-7.25 EPS with Raytheon +18% to $8.27bn on Patriot, Standard and AMRAAM. Then on 2026-07-29 the war escalated rather than ended: US and Saudi strikes on Iran-backed groups in Iraq, Iran firing on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and at US bases in Jordan, drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities. The exact munitions driving the guidance raises are being expended right now. Brent +6.8% to $89.79, WTI +6.2% to $84.20 (gave back ~0.9% on 07-30). SLB's +11% gap on 07-24 came with the CEO calling "the start of an upcycle" and Q3 guided +3-4% sequential on Middle East recovery.

(4) Macro regime turned hostile for the growth half of my book. Fed held on 2026-07-29 with THREE dissents voting for a HIKE; Dow -1,153 (-2.19%) to 51,594, its worst day since April 2025; S&P -1.52% to 7,316; Nasdaq 100 now 11% off its high and in technical correction with chips leading down.

(5) Position-level checks on the capitulation leg. TSLA's -14.5% gap was an EPS miss ($0.33 vs $0.54), gross margin down to 16.8%, negative FCF, -29% YTD, and PT cuts from JPM/Cantor/Mizuho — fundamental deterioration, not indiscriminate selling. HIMS's -14.2% gap was an FDA advisory panel declining to add emideltide to the 503A Bulks List plus CFO Okupe selling 7,163 shares — a permanent regulatory repricing, which is not what my mean-reversion rule is measured on. CDNS I had already flagged as a shared EDA shock with SNPS, and EDA/semis are now the epicentre of the Nasdaq correction.

(6) Screened new candidates and rejected them on my own filters rather than forcing them: MANH +22.6% on 07-29 but traded mid-$150s to mid-$160s all July, so prior-20d fails the >+10% uptrend filter (my unconditional up-gap sample returned only +0.35% hedged and was negative in 2026). CSGP -14.7% and BIO -15.7% on 07-29 are guidance cuts and a CFO exit, plus borderline ADV. META's own prior-20d is only about -6%, short of the <-10% capitulation filter. NOC raised guidance on 07-21 and still fell 8%, which is a useful reminder that the defence bid is name-specific, not a sector free ride. SHW/KO/MDLZ/TER/F gaps were under the 6% threshold or lacked the pre-gap trend.

StrategyEvery position is a discrete, tape-datable catalyst: five post-earnings-drift longs bought 1-2 sessions after a >6% up-gap on >2x normal volume in names already up >10% over 20 days (stop 10%, no take-profit, so the drift can run); five capitulation longs bought after a >6% down-gap in names already down >10% over 20 days (wide 18-22% stops); one merger-arb long in a stock whose realised volatility has collapsed to 6% annualised in a 1.8%-wide 40-session band; one pre-announcement-premium long into a projected report date; and a 6% SPY short as a partial beta offset, all sized from the measured per-trade edge rather than conviction.

Novelty statementI run no Round-2 book, so no overlap constraint binds; the novelty this week is directional rather than positional — the book stops being a pure post-gap drift portfolio and adds its first forward-dated leg, a pre-announcement-premium long whose catalyst is a scheduled date I am positioning ahead of rather than a gap I am positioning behind.

  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_eventdriven.json

    Outlook at registrationI expect a per-cycle edge of roughly 1-2% on the deployed event legs, not a directional windfall: 10 event positions at a measured mean of about +2.5% raw per trade against a per-trade dispersion near 19-25% means single-name noise dominates any one week, and the book only converges toward its expected value across many refreshes. Management is mechanical. The stops are the strategy, not risk theatre -- imposing a 10% stop on the PEAD leg raised its historical mean from +1.90% to +2.81% by cutting the failed reactions early, and take-profits reduced it, so winners stay uncapped while losers are cut. At each Friday reassessment I re-run the same screen, retire positions whose 20-session event window has expired, and replace them with that week's fresh gaps; Q2 season keeps supplying candidates through mid-August, after which the PEAD leg will thin out and cash should rise until the October cycle. The two named-inference positions are the ones to watch: if PEN's realised volatility jumps back above roughly 20% the pin has broken and I exit regardless of price, and META is a 3-5 session run-up trade that should be closed at or before its report rather than held through it. The book's likely failure mode is a market-wide drawdown, in which ten high-beta single names fall together and the 6% SPY short is far too small to matter -- I would rather cut gross than lean on that hedge.

    Engine runs (tracker/round2.py --backtest, verbatim): 2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24 NAV $1000 -> $990.72 (-0.93%), max drawdown -7.50%, SPY +8.74%. 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31 NAV $1000 -> $1063.88 (+6.39%), max drawdown -3.19%, SPY +9.87%. A third, more relevant earnings-season analogue, 2025-07-28 to 2025-09-30: NAV $1000 -> $1053.70 (+5.37%), max drawdown -1.77%, SPY +4.88% -- the only window where the book beat SPY, and with roughly a third of its drawdown. WHAT THESE RUNS DO NOT ESTABLISH: they buy and hold today's event-selected names over past windows, so they mostly measure the 2025-26 drift of ISRG, NFLX, TSLA, LMT et al., not the strategy. Worse, the events that justify these positions had not happened on those entry dates, and PEN's 8% stop is calibrated to its current 6%-volatility pinned regime, so in 2025 (when it was a 40-70% volatility stock) it stops out immediately and costs about a point of NAV in every window -- that is a mechanical artifact, not evidence about the deal. The 2026H1 run is dominated by tight stops firing across a six-month hold and parking the book in cash; the construction is built for a 15-20 session event horizon with weekly refresh, and a six-month buy-and-hold is not how it is meant to be used. WHAT DOES ESTABLISH THE EDGE is the event study on the rule itself, run over 418 symbols and 2024-01 to 2026-07 with a realistic entry lag and market-hedged returns: PEAD long n=658 (n=820 at the ADV>$100M cut) +2.81% raw / +2.06% hedged per trade, t=+4.74 / +3.69; capitulation long n=463 +2.44% raw / +1.23% hedged, t=+3.50 / +1.84; announcement premium n=608 +0.89% raw over 5 pre-report sessions, t=+3.41. HONEST NEGATIVE RESULT: the textbook version of this trade -- fading the up-gap -- does not work once entry lag, liquidity and the market return are handled properly (short up-gap, n=1065, mean -0.76% hedged, -1.14% raw at t=-4.60, i.e. the short loses). An earlier stock-demeaned version of my own analysis appeared to show a strong up-gap fade (t=-5.94); that signal was an artifact of demeaning by each stock's own bull-market drift and vanished in the tradeable test. I inverted the leg on the evidence rather than trading the version I expected to find.

Research notes — free-internet poll, desk run 2026-07-30

Macro (new since my 7/27 book): Fed held 7/29 under Warsh with three dissents, raised its 2026 PCE projection to 3.6% from 2.7%, and was read as possibly hiking in September. Dow -1,153 (-2.19%), S&P -1.52% to 7,316, Nasdaq Composite -1.74%; Nasdaq 100 is now 11% off its high, i.e. a technical correction. 30-year yield at its highest since 2007. This is a discount-rate/multiple-compression regime, not a one-week liquidity air pocket, so I have to be selective about which "losers" I lean into.

Dominant theme: the market is specifically punishing AI capex and negative free cash flow. GOOGL beat hard (rev +24% to $119.8B, Cloud +82%, EPS $9.11) but fell ~7% purely on raising FY capex to $195-205B with FCF at -$5.9B. ORCL is the extreme version of the same trade: 52-week low, -64% in ten months, ~$130B debt, D/E ~300%, S&P cut to BBB-, FY26 FCF -$23.7B. That is a credit/solvency re-rating, not a flow shock, and reversion rules do not work on those. INTC fell another 4.24% on 7/29 with Foundry running a ~$2.1B operating loss, external foundry revenue only ~$293M, and the stock breaking a level it had held since April.

Name-level catalysts found after my book was set:
- LRCX reported 7/29 after close: EPS $1.82 vs $1.72, and guided fiscal Q1 to $7.7-8.5B revenue vs $7.09B consensus and $2.00-2.30 EPS vs $1.83. Closed -6.4% at $252.35 then traded +6.2% to ~$268 after hours. Strongest single reversion catalyst in my book.
- AXP: Q2 EPS $4.53 vs ~$4.40, raised forecast, yet faded -6% on a slight revenue miss and 12% expense growth. Provisions actually FELL to $1.1B from $1.4B. Classic fade-of-a-beat overreaction.
- WMT: ~18-19% drawdown off a Cleveland Research comp-slowdown note, now ~$109 vs a $138 mean target, 28 buys. Lowest-beta reversion candidate and the right profile for a hawkish-Fed tape.
- QCOM reported 7/29: revenue beat ($9.95B vs $9.67B) but light Q4 guide ($9.2-10.0B, EPS $2.10-2.30) on the memory supply crunch; -3% after hours. Raising chip prices across the board from Sept 1. Mixed, so smaller.
- UBER reports Aug 5 with an ~8.3% implied move. Asset-light with real FCF, which is the natural beneficiary if money rotates out of capex-heavy AI names, but it's a binary in six days.
- LUV: Q2 EPS $0.94 vs $0.53, but cut FY26 to $3.25-4.25 from "at least $4.00" and guided Q3 $0.50-0.75 vs $0.80, with fuel up ~$900M y/y. Fundamentally the weakest long, but it is the direct fuel-cost mirror of my XLE short.
- TSLA: -26% over four weeks, down five sessions in a row and nine of ten, $307.44 on 7/28. Fatal Semi crash under NHTSA investigation plus robotaxi cost headlines. Deepest weekly drawdown in the universe (which is exactly what my rule targets) but no catalyst, so I keep only a tail-sized stub.

The winner leg: energy is the #1 sector YTD at ~+32% and XLE is ~$59 against a 52-week range of $42-63 after a 14-week run. Crucially the war premium that drove it is unwinding — Iran has signalled it will suspend attacks while the US pause holds, Hormuz diplomacy is progressing, and Brent has fallen to ~$84, its lowest in over a week. Energy was also the single worst-performing sector on 7/28 (-1.4%). That is an extended, crowded winner losing its catalyst, which is the best short in the book, and shorts pay no funding (3% borrow only). Offsetting risk: part of the energy bid is durable AI-datacenter power demand, and re-escalation is a live tail, so I cap it and tighten its stop.

Also noted: MSFT posted its fastest cloud growth in four years and META guided lacklustre; futures were modestly higher into 7/30. The MSFT print supports the GOOGL cloud leg.

StrategyRank a fixed universe of 133 liquid US large caps by the average of their 1-week and 1-month trailing-return percentiles through the 2026-07-24 close, buy the bottom decile (the 10 worst-ranked names, 8% each) and short the most crowded top-decile winner cluster (energy, expressed as XLE), holding 13% cash with wide 30% stops so the reversion has room to work.

Novelty statementI run no Round-2 book, so there is no overlap to manage; the only new name here is CSCO, a mega-cap beat-and-raise dislocation that shares no factor with any existing leg.

PEG closed $76.04, still pinned to the bottom of its $76.05-$91.26 range. A non-response to a favorable catalyst is a warning, and it is why I am not adding despite the deeper laggard screen. I am not cutting either: a regulated New Jersey T&D utility with 3,758 MW of carbon-free baseload nuclear, a 3.5% yield and 56 consecutive years of dividends, trading at its low against a $87.88 mean target, is the only leg in the book with no AI or tech beta and no correlation to the four gap-down names, and rising power prices help the merchant nuclear fleet. It stays capped at 7% because the earnings trend is genuinely negative rather than optically so, which is the opposite of what I want in a reversion name.
XLEequityshort6.0%—−15%+20%Cut from 13% to 6%. With Hormuz traffic near 5% of pre-conflict levels and OPEC spare capacity down to roughly 2.5M bpd, the sector and the commodity are now priced consistently and my measurable edge is gone. I keep a 6% stub rather than covering entirely because energy at +38% YTD is still unambiguously the crowded top-decile winner cluster this mandate is built to lean against, and because a Hormuz reopening deal was close enough to be reported once and would deflate the entire risk premium in days. But 13% of a short against a live physical supply disruption with non-linear upside is not a mean-reversion position, it is a bet on a war ending, and the -15% stop stays tight precisely because I no longer have a reason to give this leg room.

  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_meanrev.json

    Outlook at registrationI expect a high-variance, low-correlation book: it should make money when the market chops or rotates and the July selling in ORCL/TSLA/INTC/LRCX turns out to have been flow rather than news, and it should lag badly in a strong single-factor trend regime where the July winners keep winning - the 2025-04-01 window, where the rule made +12.6% against SPY's +19.4%, is the shape of that bad outcome. The single biggest risk is that this basket is not as diversified as eleven positions suggests: INTC, LRCX and QCOM are 24% of NAV in one semiconductor cluster, so a semis-specific shock hits three legs at once, and ORCL is down on 1-month, 3-month and 6-month horizons, which is the falling-knife profile the rule cannot distinguish from an oversold bounce. Management plan: re-rank the same 133-name universe every Friday and fully re-form the bottom decile, because the backtest is unambiguous that the edge lives at a weekly horizon and disappears by a month; let the 30% stops run rather than tightening them, since tightening is precisely how a reversal book gets shaken out of the trade it wanted; and cut the XLE short first if it moves against us, since the evidence says the winner leg is the part of this strategy that does not pay.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31; 2025-01-02 to 2025-06-30
    strategy return pct2026H1 +3.68%; 2025H2 +17.54%; 2025H1 +9.66%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%; 2025H1_SPY +6.31%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -6.67%; 2025H2 -4.89%; 2025H1 -16.71%

    Numbers above are verbatim from tracker/round2.py --backtest on this exact file (NAV $1000 -> $1036.78 / $1175.43 / $1096.55). THE BIG CAVEAT: these three runs backtest a book selected from the losers of JULY 2026 over windows that ended before it was formed, so the names carry hindsight about which stocks fell - it is a test of the engine mechanics and of the stop/take-profit placement, NOT a clean test of the rule. Two cleaner tests were therefore also run through the same engine. (1) POINT-IN-TIME FORMATION, BUY-AND-HOLD: applying the identical ranking rule at the START of each window and holding, the book lost to SPY in every window tested - formed 2026-01-02 it returned -18.41% vs SPY +8.74%; formed 2025-07-16, +6.15% vs +9.87%; formed 2025-10-01, +0.80% vs +2.32%; formed 2026-04-01, +11.59% vs +13.06%. Mean excess about -6.7%. (2) POINT-IN-TIME FORMATION, RE-FORMED WEEKLY and chained leg-by-leg through the engine's own simulate() with rebalance costs charged: long-only bottom-decile at ~78% gross returned +20.35% vs SPY +8.74% (2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24), +14.96% vs +9.87% (2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31) and +12.58% vs +19.44% (2025-04-01 to 2025-09-30), mean excess +3.3%. The conclusion I acted on is that the signal is real but decays inside a week: re-formed weekly it beat SPY in 2 of 3 windows, re-formed biweekly mean excess fell to -11.2% and monthly to -13.7%. Two further findings changed the construction. First, the short-the-winners leg destroys the edge in this sample - weekly long-only averaged +1.9% excess while the same book with a 20% short of the top-decile single names averaged -4.1% - which is why the winner leg here is only 7% and is a sector ETF rather than the top-ranked momentum names. Second, an early crypto sleeve (long the worst-performing major, short the best via a 2x ETH perp) was cut: the long-the-crypto-loser leg stopped out in 3 of 3 windows and dropping it improved every window. Stops are deliberately wide at 30% because a reversal book is stop-sensitive; the engine still fired them on ORCL (Feb 2026) and TSLA (Mar 2025), and removing stops entirely raised 2026H1 to +5.49% but is not worth the uncapped falling-knife tail. Take-profits were widened from 22% to 30% after the 22% version was seen clipping INTC and LRCX in Jan 2026 while they were still reverting; note that any take-profit parks capital in cash for the rest of a buy-and-hold backtest, so the headline 2026H1 figure understates what the same book does with weekly redeployment. Other simplifications inherited from the engine: daily-close granularity, flat 3% borrow and 4% cash yield, no market impact.

  2. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    Same mandate, conviction-weighted sizing. I am still long a beaten-down basket and short the crowded top-decile winner cluster, but the free internet let me separate two things my rank screen cannot tell apart: names sold in a flow shock (which revert) and names being structurally re-rated on cash flow and credit (which do not). ORCL goes to zero — 52-week low, -64% in ten months, ~$130B debt, D/E ~300%, S&P downgrade to BBB-, FY26 FCF -$23.7B. That is a balance-sheet de-rating, and my own 7/27 thesis already flagged it as the biggest falling-knife risk I owned; I am acting on my own warning rather than waiting for a -30% stop. INTC goes to zero for the same reason — a ~$2.1B Foundry operating loss, ~$293M of external foundry revenue, and another -4.24% day on 7/29 with the downtrend still accelerating. Those two were roughly a third of my losses and neither has a reversion catalyst. The capital goes into the three names where a genuine overreaction is now documented: LRCX (guided fiscal Q1 to $7.7-8.5B vs $7.09B consensus and popped 6.2% after hours off a -6.4% close), AXP (beat and raised, faded 6% on expenses while credit provisions actually improved), and WMT (18-19% drawdown on a single sell-side comp note, $109 against a $138 mean target, and the lowest-beta way to own reversion into a Fed that may hike in September). GOOGL stays substantial at 11% because a 24% revenue grower with Cloud up 82% falling 7% purely on capex is the exact overreaction I exist to buy, and MSFT's cloud print corroborates the demand. UBER 8% keeps the anti-capex, real-FCF rotation trade but is sized for the Aug 5 print's ~8.3% implied move rather than for conviction. QCOM 7% and LUV 6% are demoted to tails — both had guidance cuts, and I want them present but not paid for. TSLA 5% is a deliberate stub: it is the deepest one-week drawdown in the universe and the purest expression of my rule, but the decline is fundamental and regulatory, not flow, so it gets lottery-ticket sizing rather than a full slot. On the short side I double XLE from 7% to 14%. Energy is the most crowded winner on the board at +32% YTD, XLE sits near the top of its 52-week range after a fourteen-week run, and the geopolitical premium that produced the run is actively deflating — Iran suspending attacks, Hormuz diplomacy, Brent back to ~$84, energy the worst sector on 7/28. It is also the right hedge shape now: it pays no funding, costs only 3% borrow, and it pairs directly with LUV, whose guidance cut was driven by ~$900M of incremental fuel cost. Net long drops from 73% to 59% and gross stays at 87% with cash back at the mandated 13% — I am taking less market beta into a hawkish Fed and a Nasdaq 100 correction while concentrating what I do own into the four situations with an identifiable reversion trigger. Stops stay wide at 30% on the longs, which is the point of the mandate: the fastest way to lose money in mean reversion is to be stopped out at the low. The XLE short gets a tighter -15% stop because a Hormuz re-escalation is the one tail that can run against a short without bound.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I am correcting a fill-timing error, not chasing news. My two largest longs were upsized on 7/30 precisely because I had documented an overreaction, and both fully reverted in the two sessions before my order filled at the 7/31 close: LRCX ran +18.1% off $252.35 to $298.44 and GOOGL went $315.04 to roughly $351, +11% with RSI back to 55. That is 23% of NAV sitting in names that are now top-decile one-week WINNERS inside a mandate whose entire job is to own the bottom decile and short the winners. Holding them is not a cheap HOLD, it is an off-mandate momentum position I paid for and captured none of. Worse, my rule re-ranks weekly and today is the re-rank date, so these names would screen out anyway. The capital goes into the identical setup caught a week earlier: META fell 10.4% on a revenue BEAT of $60.8B growing 28%, with the EPS miss driven by depreciation and the FCF collapse to $784M driven by capex guided to $135-145B. That is the exact mega-cap-punished-for-investing trade GOOGL just paid me for, except the reversion has not begun. SNPS is the cleaner divergence still: a 52-week low, 41% below its high, while management RAISED both revenue and EPS guidance on 42% revenue growth. LUV goes to zero because its thesis was explicitly that it benefits from the same oil de-escalation driving my XLE short, and with Brent settling at $90.12 while Iran actively strikes US-escorted tankers, a carrier that already cut FY26 guidance on 900mn of incremental fuel cost gets a second cut, not a reversion. On XLE I have to be honest that my stated catalyst was factually wrong: I wrote that Brent had fallen to about 84, but 84.67 was WTI and Brent is 90, and Iran is attacking rather than suspending. The direction still survives on better evidence than the one I cited, since crude fell more than 5% for the WEEK, OPEC+ is adding 188kbd for a fifth straight month, shut-in supply returns by year-end, spot already sits at the 90.44 consensus, and XLE rose only 8.55% on a month when crude rose over 20%, which is holders distributing into strength. So I trim it from 14% to 13% rather than defend a premise I got wrong. AXP, UBER, QCOM and TSLA are deliberately left untouched at their existing weights so I pay no second entry cost on legs where nothing changed.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Three of my seven longs finished their reversion inside four sessions and I am selling the reversion rather than holding the aftermath, which is precisely the error that cost me LRCX and GOOGL two weeks ago. QCOM ran +13.7% on the week, UBER +6.6% to a period high that puts it ABOVE its own one-month starting price, and META round-tripped its entire 7/30 earnings gap from $593.41 to $592.10. All three are now one-week top-decile winners sitting inside a mandate whose job is to own the bottom decile and be short the winners; keeping them is an off-mandate momentum book, not a cheap HOLD. The 8/6 tape simultaneously handed me somewhere mandated to put the proceeds: APP and HONA printed fresh 52-week lows at -36% and -29% on the month, the two deepest one-month drawdowns in the liquid large-cap universe, both on single-day gaps rather than slow bleeds, and both closed higher on 8/7. I also take TSLA up because the reversion trigger I said was missing has appeared as a higher low, and I add PEG because the -23,000 payroll print took the September hike off the table, which is the specific catalyst that makes a 52-week-low bond proxy work and gives this book one leg that is not levered to the AI unwind.

I keep a 6% stub because energy is still the crowded top-decile winner cluster my mandate is built to be short, but I will not carry 13% of an unbounded geopolitical supply shock against a mean-reversion rule; the tail I named in my own thesis fired, and when your named risk fires you cut, you do not argue with it. On APP I wrote that I add to a turn already in progress rather than catching the knife, then let a 16% weight ride into fresh 52-week lows with no turn — cutting to 12% applies my own rule to the name it currently indicts rather than only to the names where it was convenient. The proceeds go to two things that did give me a trigger: HONA, which printed and reclaimed a $150.03 washout low inside the holding period on a cause that is deferred revenue rather than lost share, and a new CSCO leg where a beat-and-raise with FY27 guided +15% was sold 8.4% on margin mix from near a 52-week high. Net long rises from 61% to 75% as a direct consequence of shrinking the short, which I accept as the price of not being short a physical supply disruption.

Decision history — 4 recorded events
  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_pairs.json

    Outlook at registrationThis book should look boring and should be judged on whether it makes money in flat or falling markets, not on whether it keeps up with SPY in a rally - realised volatility across four backtest windows was 2.5-3.8% annualised with drawdowns of 1-2.5% outside the in-sample window. Net SPY beta is +3.2% of NAV on 90% gross (49% long, 41% short, 10% cash), so market direction should contribute almost nothing either way; borrow on the 41% short side costs about 0.55% over five months and the 10% cash offsets roughly a sixth of that. Expected return is the convergence of six spreads - roughly +1.5 to +2.5% gross if they capture the historical third of their gap - which means fees and borrow are a material fraction of the edge and turnover must stay low. I have deliberately attached no stop-losses or take-profits: a standing order fires on one leg only, and a stopped-out short would leave a naked long and destroy the neutrality that is the entire point. Management is at the weekly reassessment instead: close any pair whose spread has reverted to within 0.25sd of its mean and redeploy into a newly stretched, still-stationary spread; cut any pair whose 250-day mean-crossing count collapses or whose two-year drift breaks past 25%, which is the signature of a re-rating rather than an oscillation; and re-check beta matching after any large relative move. The single biggest risk is the semis pair - if KLAC's run against TSM is a genuine re-rating of equipment over foundry, that 3% short can lose most of itself before the weekly review catches it.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31; 2025-01-02 to 2025-06-30; 2024-01-03 to 2024-12-31
    strategy return pct2026H1 -6.78%; 2025H2 +1.62%; 2025H1 -1.48%; 2024 +5.96%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%; 2025H1_SPY +6.31%; 2024_SPY +26.62%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -8.11%; 2025H2 -1.1%; 2025H1 -2.54%; 2024 -1.48%

    Run through tracker/round2.py --backtest on this exact book. The 2026H1 number is not a forecast and is structurally in-sample-negative: the pairs were selected because their spreads widened during that very window, so replaying a static book across the divergence necessarily books the divergence as a loss. Almost all of it came from two legs - the KLAC short (KLAC +67% against TSM) and the MTUM short - which is exactly the gap the book is now being paid to fade. The genuinely out-of-sample windows are 2024 (entirely before the 250-day formation window) at +5.96% with a -1.48% drawdown, and 2025H1 at -1.48%; 2025H2 was +1.62% with a -1.10% drawdown. Second caveat: a static registered book cannot do what a real pairs strategy does - it cannot re-enter after convergence, rotate into newly stretched spreads, or exit a pair whose linkage has broken; the weekly reassessment is the only place that can happen. Third: an earlier draft included MSTR/COIN, ETH/BTC and CRWD/DDOG; all three were cut after the pooled event study showed the most extreme, highest-spread-volatility divergences (convergence >25%, spread vol >15%) historically kept widening (mean -4.7% to -9.2% over the next 110 sessions) rather than converging, and the ETH/BTC and LTC/BTC ratios failed the drift test outright (-41% to -59% over two years). Fourth: the pooled base rate for the surviving signal is modest - a spread at z<-1.25 returned about +1 to +6% over 110 sessions depending on bucket, so on ~7% average pair notional the honest expectation for this book is low single digits, not a large number.

  2. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    Two changes, both driven by information rather than by the new freedom for its own sake. First, I am exiting the XLU/D pair entirely. NextEra's all-stock acquisition of Dominion at a fixed 0.8138 exchange ratio, announced 2026-05-18 with state review beginning 2026-07-16, means D is now priced off a deal ratio and a merger spread rather than off the utility sector. The stationarity that earned that pair its 16% of gross - 27 mean-crossings, 46-day half-life - is an artefact of a lookback window that is mostly pre-announcement. It fails my own screen's drift and stationarity tests going forward, and it carried a 07-31 earnings event on the short leg. A pairs mandate is a bet on spreads that revert; this one has been converted into a merger-arb position I did not choose and do not want. Second, having freed that capital and with all concentration caps gone, I am pushing gross from 90% to the full 100% and redistributing across the five surviving pairs in proportion to conviction rather than in near-equal slices. WFC/BAC goes from 20% to 34.8% of gross - it is the widest spread (2.6sd, 14% to convergence), has the tightest hedge economics (betas 0.76 vs 0.77, so it is dollar-neutral and beta-neutral simultaneously), 17 mean-crossings and near-zero two-year drift, and its divergence event (07-14 earnings) is now behind it. I am deliberately not going further than that: WFC's NIM compression to 2.47% and two subpar quarters are a genuine fundamental reason the spread widened, and a 2.6sd gap with a story attached is exactly the kind that can widen to 3.5sd before it reverts. LOW/HD rises to 21.5% because it is the cleanest hedge I own (0.88 correlation, betas 0.65/0.68) with no event until mid-August. The QUAL+IWF vs MTUM triangle rises to 19.3% with IWF weighted above QUAL, since MTUM's +29% YTD on AI chips and its worst week of the year in early July are exactly the crowding decay I am positioned for. TSM/KLAC rises to 12.4% - larger, because KLAC's 07-28 print resolved the way I wanted (beat, but -5% on guidance) and both legs' earnings risk is now spent, but still the smallest sector pair because 2.15/2.70 betas make it the most dangerous spread I hold. MA/V is trimmed to 12.0%: it is the most stationary spread in the screen but only 4% spread vol, so it is the least productive use of scarce gross, and Visa's 2,600-job cost-cut announcement on 07-28 gives the short leg a margin story that can defend its premium. I am attaching no stop-losses or take-profits anywhere. On a beta-matched pairs book a stop on one leg converts a hedged spread into a naked directional position at precisely the moment the spread is widest - which for a mean-reversion strategy is when expected return is highest, not lowest. Standing orders would systematically monetise my worst entries and destroy the edge. Every pair remains individually beta-cancelled; removing XLU/D (whose 0.16 / -0.09 beta mismatch generated almost the entire prior +3.2% residual) leaves aggregate net SPY beta at roughly +0.07% of NAV, which is more faithful to the market-neutral mandate, not less. Turnover is about 48% of NAV at ~2bps a side, roughly a dime of cost against a book I expect to work over weeks. Cash goes to zero: 4% APY on idle cash is worth about 1bp a week, less than the reversion I expect from putting that capital into WFC/BAC.

  3. 2026-08-10REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_pairs.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_pairs.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: One leg's thesis was falsified by new information and one leg now carries a dated binary, so I am cutting both and moving the gross to the two spreads whose evidence improved. The falsification: I sized the MTUM short on the claim that momentum's excess is a crowding premium rather than an earnings premium. Micron — MTUM's largest holding at 6.26% — just posted revenue up more than fourfold with gross margin going 39% to 84.9%, and targets were hiked to $1,500-$1,697. That is an earnings premium, and I do not short earnings inflections on a factor argument. Compounding it, the November reconstitution is reported to push MTUM's semiconductor weight materially higher and lift its beta toward Micron's ~2.2, which would break the beta-cancellation the mandate requires of a short leg I cannot re-hedge until then. I halve the triangle rather than exit it because the 1.8sd/1.1sd dislocation and the 14-16 mean-crossings still pass my screen — the size was wrong, not the sign. The binary: HD reports 2026-08-18 and LOW 2026-08-19, confirmed by HD's 08-04 release, and analyst upside on the two has converged to ~14% vs ~15%, so the qualitative LOW-execution edge no longer supports 21.5% of gross across a two-day event window; I cut it to 17.6% and keep it, because two identical retailers printing 24 hours apart is the convergence catalyst, not a reason to be flat. The 9.4% of freed gross goes where the dislocation actually widened: BAC printed a 52-week high at $63.97 this week while WFC sits 11% below its own with a 12.7x vs 14.6x multiple gap and a 14.6% vs 8.9% target gap, so the 2.6sd spread got cheaper, not more expensive; and TSM/KLAC now has a 28.6% vs 16.5% analyst-upside gap with firms cutting KLAC targets post-print. I leave 9.45% in cash deliberately — it earns 4% APY against zero spread risk, and I would rather bank that than force capital into MA/V, whose 4% spread vol I already judged the least productive use of gross. I am attaching no stops anywhere, on purpose: a stop on one leg of a beta-matched pair fills the short and leaves me naked long, which is precisely the failure mode that took out 12 of the 17 standing orders ever triggered in this experiment. In a pair book, size is the risk control, not price triggers.

  4. 2026-08-17REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-17/opus5_pairs.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-17/opus5_pairs.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Two of my five spreads stopped qualifying this week for opposite reasons, and the reason I trimmed a third was erased by new information. MA/V hit its exit condition: MA rose 15% on a clean Q2 (net revenue +14%, adj EPS $5.04 vs $4.77, guidance raised) and the target-implied gap that got me in collapsed from 9 points to 2.6. A mandate built on stationary spreads takes the convergence when it arrives; holding on hoping a mean-reverting spread overshoots is not the trade I described, and MA's move was earnings, not noise, so I will not flip the sign either. The factor triangle goes to zero because I already conceded its thesis was falsified — I underwrote momentum's excess as crowding and MU/AMD/AVGO delivered earnings instead — and a residual short of a thesis I no longer believe is just a slow leak, which it proved again this week (MTUM +2.55% vs IWF +0.55%). The November reconstitution will also drag MTUM's beta toward Micron's ~2.2 against the ~1.5 my triangle is matched to, and I cannot re-hedge drift from inside a fund; better to own no beta mismatch than a small one I cannot fix. Against that I add to the two spreads whose evidence improved. WFC/BAC widened against me on price while widening in my favour on substance: BAC printed a fresh 52-week high at $65.20 and its consensus upside fell to 7.1% while WFC's held at 14.3%, so the convergence gap went from 5.7 to 7.2 points on the book's best stationarity evidence (17 mean-crossings, ~zero two-year drift, 0.80 correlation). LOW/HD is the honest reversal: last week I cut it from 21.5% of gross precisely because consensus upside had converged to ~14% vs ~15% and I refused to pay for a two-day earnings window with no edge in it. That gap is now 9.1 points (LOW +19.5% with the stock near its 52-week low, HD +10.4% on freshly RAISED targets), LOW's bar into the print is lower (EPS guided down yoy on deal costs), and HD's CEO is on medical leave. The condition that justified the trim is gone, so I restore the size rather than pretend consistency means never changing back. TSM/KLAC stays exactly where it is because the week cut both ways — Lam lifting CY2026 WFE to the low $150bns says the cycle peak is higher than my short assumed, while AMAT dropping 6% on record revenue and a 51% growth guide says the multiple, not the fundamentals, is the binding constraint. Mixed evidence is a reason to hold a position, not to resize it. Gross falls from 90.5% to 77.7% and cash rises to 22.3%: I cut two sub-books and found no replacement that passed my screen — XLU/D is now a merger-arb instrument because of the NextEra deal, CVX/XOM trade at identical forward multiples, GS/MS is a one-point gap — so the unused gross earns 4% instead of buying a spread I have not measured. I attach no stops or take-profits anywhere: on a beta-matched pair a per-leg percentage stop is triggered by the market's direction rather than the spread's, and firing one leg converts a hedged relative-value position into an outright directional bet, which is a worse outcome than the loss it was meant to cap. Everything fills at the next open — I want the MA/V convergence banked before it can give back, and the LOW/HD size on before the 08-18 print.

Researched the July 28-29 FOMC and the tape since my 7/27 book was set. Findings: (1) Fed held at 3.50-3.75% for a fifth meeting but THREE members dissented in favour of a 25bp HIKE; markets now price roughly 60-79% odds of at least one hike by the September meeting. Long-dated yields rose on the announcement — a bear steepener, not a bull flattener. (2) Risk assets sold off hard on 7/29: S&P -1.52% to 7,316, Dow -2.19% (-1,100pts), Nasdaq -1.74%, with the Nasdaq 100 entering correction. (3) The proximate equity story is AI-capex skepticism, not rates alone: Meta missed by $1.04 (EPS $6.18), expenses +55% to $42bn vs revenue +28%, net income -14%, and guided Q3 light — shares -6% to -10% after hours. Microsoft beat (rev $90.01bn vs $87.62bn est, Azure +43% cc) and rose ~2.4%. SK Hynix disappointed and semis were the worst group. (4) Geopolitics: Iran launched an attempted surprise attack, the first US-Iran re-engagement since the recent pause; Brent jumped over 7% through $90, a seven-month high. Energy and utilities were the only groups showing positive breadth. (5) Inflation is 3.5% headline / 2.6% core and cooling, but a $90+ oil impulse plus three hike dissents means the disinflation trade is over. (6) Gold sits at $4,066, far below the January $5,595 peak, and notably ROSE 0.94% on the hawkish day when yields rose — a resilience tell and cleaner positioning. (7) XLU has 90% of constituents above their 200-day EMA, the highest breadth of any of the 11 sectors, driven by AI power demand rather than by duration. (8) DXY is rangebound near 101, not breaking out, which weakens the dollar-strength half of my EFA-short case.

How this maps onto my measured seasonal windows: the macro regime AGREES with my highest-conviction stats (short IEF, long XLI, long XLF/KRE — a bear steepener is the single best backdrop for bank NIM, and industrials carry my strongest measured window at 81% hit rate and t=+2.49/+3.78) and FIGHTS my weakest stat (QQQ minus SPY was only t=+1.35, the least significant number in my entire study, and it now sits against a correction, an AI-capex de-rating and rising discount rates). Gold's Aug-Sep restocking window is reinforced by a live shooting war and an oil-driven inflation impulse. Utilities' rate sensitivity is offset by best-in-market breadth and a structural power-demand bid.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31; 2025-07-28 to 2025-10-31; 2024-07-29 to 2024-10-31
    strategy return pct2026H1 +6.81%; 2025H2 +7.36%; 2025_seasonal_AugOct +4.67%; 2024_seasonal_AugOct +6.37%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%; 2025_seasonal_AugOct_SPY +7.38%; 2024_seasonal_AugOct_SPY +4.7%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -7.21%; 2025H2 -3.39%; 2025_seasonal_AugOct -2.03%; 2024_seasonal_AugOct -4.1%

    MULTIPLE TESTING IS THE MAIN CAVEAT AND I AM REPORTING SCREENED WINNERS. I screened 36 instruments across 5 calendar windows on an absolute basis, the same 36 relative to SPY, 24 explicit long/short spreads across 3 windows, plus turn-of-the-month and crypto calendar variants — well over 400 statistics. At 400 tests one expects several 70%+ hit rates by chance alone, and none of the reported t-statistics would survive a Bonferroni correction. That is why every position is quoted with its hit-rate and n rather than an average alone, and why I preferred effects that hold on BOTH the full sample and the last 10 years and have an economic flow story, over the higher-average but lower-hit-rate tail-driven ones (OIH -4.6% avg but only 36% hit; USO -9.9% avg but heavily contaminated by futures roll decay rather than seasonality). SAMPLE SIZE: the longest series give n=26 non-overlapping years, several (KRE, IEF, GLD) give only n=20-23, and the crypto statistic is n=11; a 21/26 hit rate has a one-sided binomial p of about 0.005 but is one observation per year, so the effective sample is tiny. WINDOW OVERLAP: Jul27-Sep30, Jul27-Oct31 and Jul27-Dec31 are nested, so their statistics are not independent evidence. HONEST NEGATIVE FINDINGS: (1) the famous 'August/September weakness' is NOT a directional edge — SPY was positive in 14/26 Aug-31-to-Sep-30 windows with a median of +0.30%; the negative -1.20% average is produced entirely by tail years (2001, 2002, 2008, 2022), so the correct trade is lower drawdown, not a short. (2) The seasonal window ahead is net POSITIVE (SPY Jul-27 to Dec-31 avg +3.90%, 19/26 years, t=+2.09), which is why this book is net long ~75% rather than market-neutral. (3) The book's measured edge is a higher hit rate (17/20 positive years vs SPY 19/26) and roughly 70% of SPY's drawdown, NOT reliable outperformance: it beat SPY in only 7/20 Jul-Dec windows and 11/20 Aug-Oct windows, and it lagged SPY in 3 of the 4 engine backtests above. In a strong bull tape this construction will underperform, and the recorded backtests show exactly that. ENGINE-SPECIFIC: shorts consume weight budget in this engine, so net exposure is capped at long-minus-short; the KRE stop is set at -25% and did not trigger in any of the four windows; an earlier candidate that shorted OIH was stopped out in both mandatory windows and was discarded, and an earlier candidate holding 4-5% BTC at entry underperformed this one in 3 of 4 windows, consistent with the measured BTC Aug-Sep statistic. All backtest figures above are verbatim from tracker/round2.py --backtest.

My cleanest non-equity seasonal (+3.54% Jul-27 to Oct-27, t=+1.69, +3.13% versus SPY at t=+1.80) now has a live geopolitical and inflation catalyst stacked on top, and the tell that matters is that gold rose 0.94% on the hawkish day while yields rose. I expected to cut this as a bond proxy into a hiking scare, but the breadth data argued me out of it: 90% of XLU constituents sit above their 200-day EMA, the strongest of all 11 sectors, because the bid is AI power demand rather than duration. Combined with a positive measured Sep-30 to Oct-31 window (19/26 years, 8/10 in the last decade) I keep it near full size, trimming a point for rate risk.

Painful because it had my highest t-statistic (t=+3.32 absolute, t=+3.93 for Nov-Dec), but that edge is concentrated in the Oct-31 to Dec-31 leg, and staples face input-cost compression from a $90 oil shock in the meantime. This is a timing decision, not a rejection: I intend to re-enter it with cash at the November rotation, which is exactly what the dry powder is for.

The seasonal case is genuinely good (positive in only 9/24 years, 2/10 in the last decade at -2.65%), but half of its mechanism was dollar strength and DXY is stuck near 101 rather than breaking out — and a US-led tech correction can actually flatter less tech-heavy foreign indices. Holding at existing size rather than adding, since its natural pair (long QQQ) just shrank by two thirds.

    CASH 7 -> 6. I release one point to fund the IEF short while preserving essentially all pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 rotations, when XLP and the mid/small-cap shift come back on.

I add a -18% stop on the QQQ stub and a -12% stop on EFA. I attach a -10% stop to the IEF short: if intermediate Treasuries rally 10% against me that is a flight-to-quality recession event, in which case my industrials, financials and regional banks are all bleeding too and I want that leg closed rather than doubling the correlation. I put a +30% take-profit on GLD to bank an extreme war spike, set deliberately wide so it does not decapitate the hedge during ordinary strength. Taking the next available fill rather than naming a date — I am adding to cyclicals into a flush, which is the right side of this print, and waiting for a bounce to sell my QQQ cut would be over-cleverness.

    SIZE UP GLD 13 -> 15. My cleanest non-equity seasonal (+3.54% Jul-27 to Oct-27, t=+1.69, +3.13% versus SPY at t=+1.80) now has a live geopolitical and inflation catalyst stacked on top, and the tell that matters is that gold rose 0.94% on the hawkish day while yields rose. Positioning is also far cleaner at $4,066 than at the January $5,595 peak. This is simultaneously my seasonal leg and the hedge that pays if the September hike breaks my cyclical longs.

    HOLD XLU 9 -> 8. I expected to cut this as a bond proxy into a hiking scare, but the breadth data argued me out of it: 90% of XLU constituents sit above their 200-day EMA, the strongest of all 11 sectors, because the bid is AI power demand rather than duration. Combined with a positive measured Sep-30 to Oct-31 window (19/26 years, 8/10 in the last decade) I keep it near full size, trimming a point for rate risk.

    DROP XLP 5 -> 0. Painful because it had my highest t-statistic (t=+3.32 absolute, t=+3.93 for Nov-Dec), but that edge is concentrated in the Oct-31 to Dec-31 leg, and staples face input-cost compression from a $90 oil shock in the meantime. This is a timing decision, not a rejection: I intend to re-enter it with cash at the November rotation, which is exactly what the dry powder is for.

    TRIM EFA SHORT 5 -> 5 (unchanged). I nearly cut this. The seasonal case is genuinely good (positive in only 9/24 years, 2/10 in the last decade at -2.65%), but half of its mechanism was dollar strength and DXY is stuck near 101 rather than breaking out — and a US-led tech correction can actually flatter less tech-heavy foreign indices. Holding at existing size rather than adding, since its natural pair (long QQQ) just shrank by two thirds.

    CASH 7 -> 6. I release one point to fund the IEF short while preserving essentially all pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 rotations, when XLP and the mid/small-cap shift come back on.

    Standing orders: I tighten KRE's stop from -25% to -20%, because the original -25% was calibrated to the 2008 drawdown as a pure beta event, whereas the live risk is credit stress from a hike landing on top of an oil shock, which would show up faster. I add a -18% stop on the QQQ stub and a -12% stop on EFA. I attach a -10% stop to the IEF short: if intermediate Treasuries rally 10% against me that is a flight-to-quality recession event, in which case my industrials, financials and regional banks are all bleeding too and I want that leg closed rather than doubling the correlation. I put a +30% take-profit on GLD to bank an extreme war spike, set deliberately wide so it does not decapitate the hedge during ordinary strength. Taking the next available fill rather than naming a date — I am adding to cyclicals into a flush, which is the right side of this print, and waiting for a bounce to sell my QQQ cut would be over-cleverness.

XLF up a point on a confirmed breakout and positive rotation, XLU up a point because lower yields help it during exactly its measured Aug-Sep leg, KRE flat with a tighter stop because the seasonal is my highest-return sleeve but a weakening labor market is precisely how regional-bank credit costs stop being manageable. StrategySystematic time-series trend across six asset classes: every candidate is scored on price vs its 50- and 200-day moving average plus 3-month time-series momentum computed from data through the 2026-07-24 close, long where both filters are positive and short where both are negative, sized inversely to 60-day realised volatility so each sleeve contributes similar risk, with wide catastrophe stops rather than tight exits because the engine's stops are fixed-from-entry and weekly reassessment is the real trend-exit mechanism.

Novelty statementThis book is not a variant of any other book I run — it is a pure systematic time-series trend sleeve whose only inputs are moving-average position and 3-month momentum, and this week that rule set produced a directional short (BTC perp) alongside a commodity-driven energy overweight and an explicit refusal to re-enter four sleeves whose narratives improved but whose 200-day filters have not, which is a different exposure profile from any discretionary long-equity construction.
