  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_trend.json

    Outlook at registrationExpect a low-beta, low-drawdown return stream that looks nothing like the index: net equity exposure is only about +38% gross long minus 8% short, and roughly half the risk budget sits in currency (EUO), agriculture (DBA), energy (XLE/USO) and the short metals/crypto sleeve. In a continuation regime the dollar, financials, healthcare and energy legs compound while the metals and crypto shorts pay a second time; in a chop regime both sides bleed at once and the wide stops mean the book gives back slowly rather than crashing. Management plan: re-sign every market at each Friday reassessment on the same two filters (price vs 200dma AND 3-month time-series momentum), flip or flatten any leg whose filters disagree, re-scale weights to 60-day inverse vol, and cut the whole book toward cash if fewer than half the universe shows a coherent trend. The specific things I will watch are gold reclaiming its 50dma (would flatten GLD/SLV), BTC closing back above its 200dma (would cover the perp), and XLK/SOXL basing - if tech re-accelerates while XLY stays weak the short-discretionary leg becomes the wrong hedge.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31; 2025-01-02 to 2025-06-30
    strategy return pct2026H1 +12.55%; 2025H2 +1.83%; 2025H1 -6.14%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%; 2025H1_SPY +6.31%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -3.25%; 2025H2 -3.93%; 2025H1 -9.42%

    Run through tracker/round2.py --backtest on this exact file; numbers verbatim. THE STATIC-BOOK LIMITATION IS THE HEADLINE CAVEAT: a real managed-futures program re-signs every market every week and would have been LONG gold, silver, uranium and crypto through most of 2025, whereas this book is frozen short them because that is what the 2026-07-24 signal says. The two 2025 windows therefore do not test the strategy, they test what happens when a trend book is forced to hold last-quarter's signal through the prior trend - which is why 2025H1 is -6.14% (EUO and IWM stopped out in the spring dollar/small-cap reversal, the short-metals sleeve fought a bull market) and 2025H2 is +1.83% with all four metals/crypto shorts stopped or taken out. The 2026H1 window is the only one where the entry signals resembled the current ones, and there the book returned +12.55% against SPY +8.74% with a -3.25% drawdown, i.e. it beat the index at roughly a third of its volatility. Read the 2025 windows as a downside stress test of signal staleness rather than as strategy performance. Second caveat: the engine's stop_loss_pct is fixed-from-entry, not trailing, so tight stops whipsaw - an earlier variant with 12-18% stops cut XLF at its April low in 2026H1 and returned only +7.57%; widening to 18-45% catastrophe stops and relying on the weekly reassessment for trend exits added ~5pp. Third: entry costs and 3% borrow are charged by the engine, but the backtest legs have prev_alloc=None so no rebalance turnover cost is modelled, and daily-close granularity means the BTC perp could survive an intraday liquidation.

  2. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    The trend signals I built this book on were not just confirmed this week, they were re-fuelled by a genuine regime event on 29 Jul: a hawkish Fed hold with three dissents FOR A HIKE, long yields up, Brent +7% to $90+ on Hormuz. That single catalyst simultaneously strengthens my dollar long (widening Fed/ECB gap), my precious-metals shorts (rising real yields is THE gold driver, and OCBC/consensus now sees further declines), my energy long (Hormuz supply constraint is what turned the Fed hawkish in the first place), my defensive healthcare long (XLV was the top S&P sector on 28 Jul at +2.33% while the index fell 1.5%), and my consumer-discretionary short (4.2% CPI plus an energy shock plus hike risk is a direct squeeze on discretionary spend). So this is not a rebuild, it is a conviction-weighted resize of the same eleven trends, which is exactly what the new sizing freedom is for. Three changes. FIRST, I EXIT IWM ENTIRELY. It was already my weakest signal (only 0.1% above its 50dma, i.e. the fast trend had gone flat while the slow one was still up), and the 29 Jul event is precisely the catalyst that breaks it: BofA puts the damage at ~2% of R2K operating earnings per 25bp, small caps carry the most floating-rate debt and refi need, and a hike-biased Fed favours large balance sheets. Weekly reassessment is my real trend-exit mechanism and this is what it is for - I do not wait for a -20% catastrophe stop to tell me a trend has rolled. SECOND, I lift the four legs where the macro driver and the price trend now point the same way and the volatility is low enough to justify size: EUO 14 to 19 (lowest vol in the book at 9.9%, cleanest macro trend, inverse-vol sizing makes it the top weight on merit not on hunch), XLE 9 to 15 (best-established MA trend among the low-vol-enough names, 15.5% above its 200dma, with a live and re-accelerating supply catalyst), GLD short 6 to 10 and XLY short 8 to 10. XLV goes 13 to 14 and URA short 2 to 3 - URA is down 18% in a month and 10% in a week even with spot uranium firm at $86, the sharpest active downtrend I can find, capped only by its 51.8% vol. THIRD, I trim XLF 16 to 10. The trend is genuinely intact (record high $56.18, +8.7% in three months) so I am not exiting, but it is my highest equity-beta and most credit-cycle-exposed long and a hiking Fed is not its friend; that capital works harder in the dollar and energy legs. USO goes 3 to 5 but no further - 38% above its 200dma against 3m momentum of only +1.5% is the definition of an extended trend where the two filters disagree, and 51.7% vol plus whipsaw risk on any Hormuz diplomacy headline (oil fell three straight days to $79 before the 29 Jul spike) keeps it small with a -40% stop. I am NOT going to a one-line book. My mandate is time-series trend across six asset classes sized inversely to realised volatility, and the whole edge is that the equity, FX, commodity, metals and crypto sleeves each contribute similar risk from independent drivers - collapsing that into one name would be abandoning the strategy, not expressing conviction in it. Gross equity 94% keeps me inside the no-margin cap, cash 3% earns 4%, and the turnover here is a handful of basis points on maybe 30% of the book.

  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_unrestricted.json

    Outlook at registrationI expect this book to make money in the 8-20% range over the rest of 2026 if the oil supply regime holds, driven mostly by the ERX/MPC core, and to lose 8-12% if crude round-trips - the asymmetry comes from energy equities having repriced only about a third of the crude move, so they have far less to give back than crude does. Realised book vol on 2026 data is 11.4% annualised at a -0.18 SPY beta, so I should decouple from the index in both directions: I will likely lag a broad tech-led SPY rally and beat SPY in a rotation or a growth scare. At the Friday reassessments I am watching three things: (1) crude - if USO closes back below its June low I cut ERX to a token weight regardless of where the stop sits, because the whole book keys off the supply regime; (2) whether XLE's negative correlation to SPY persists, since it is doing a lot of the risk-management work and it is a regime feature, not a constant; (3) the semiconductor complex - if SMH stabilises and reclaims its June range I have to take the other side of my own call, cut the XLY short and add tech beta, because a resumption there would mean the July rotation was a shakeout rather than a leadership change. The risk I am most worried about is not the one the stops cover. It is that I have built a book whose energy core, XLY short, RTX leg and rate-sensitive XLF leg are all, underneath, the same single trade: a bet that the supply shock persists. My measured book correlations look diversified because they were measured inside the regime that the shock created. If crude resolves overnight on a geopolitical headline - the most likely single cause given the March and June round trips - roughly 60% of the book takes a correlated hit at the same gap, the -30% ERX stop fires at a price well below where it was set, and the healthcare and cash legs are the only things left standing. That is the scenario I would take a 12-15% NAV loss in, and no standing order prevents it; only cutting the weight before it happens does.

    All figures are verbatim from tracker/round2.py --backtest on this exact construction. BE CLEAR ABOUT WHAT THIS IS AND IS NOT EVIDENCE FOR. The 2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24 window is almost entirely hindsight-contaminated and should be read as a construction check, not a result: ERX and MPC were selected precisely because energy led 2026, and XLV, XLF, RTX and AAPL were all picked off a trailing 3-month/1-month momentum screen run through the 2026-07-24 close, so every long leg knows the answer. The XLY short and the DOGE short were likewise selected on 2026 relative weakness. The +31.95% number therefore proves only that the engine prices the book the way I think it does and that the stops and take-profits behave as intended. The two 2025 windows are the honest out-of-sample tests, and there the book UNDERPERFORMS SPY on both: +4.33% vs +9.87% in 2025H2 and +5.25% vs +6.31% in 2025H1, the latter with a -13.19% drawdown against a +6.31% SPY. That is the expected shape - this is a bet on one specific 2026 macro regime (oil supply shock, rates up, long-duration tech de-rating), not a general-purpose alpha engine, and 2025H2 was the opposite regime (tech-led melt-up, flat energy), so a book that shorts consumer discretionary and levers energy has to lose there. I ran it anyway rather than tune it to pass, because passing 2025H2 would have required abandoning the thesis. Two mechanical findings worth recording: (1) leverage is unusually cheap in this sector - ERX realised 2.01x XLE on the year and 2.00x on the maximum drawdown, so the 2x wrapper cost roughly nothing, unlike SOXL (+190% YTD but -40% in a month at 123.6% vol) or FAS (0.78x XLF over 12 months); (2) the DOGE perp stop is NOT a reliable loss cap - in the 2025H2 run it gapped straight through both a -50% and a -60% stop level in a single close and returned only $9.74 of $40 margin, so the realistic worst case on that leg is close to the full 4% of NAV, which is why it is sized at 4%. Across the three windows the DOGE leg contributed +4.6pp, -3.1pp and +3.65pp versus an otherwise identical book without it. Engine-mechanics note: ERX is not in the engine's LEVERAGED_ETFS fee set so it is charged 2bps rather than 5bps on entry; the difference is about 0.7bps of NAV and the construction does not depend on it.

    Stated reason (desk log)

    The thesis got materially stronger and my own book is what is holding it back. Since 27 July the account has made +0.36% while the mandate's core driver went vertical — crude +6.2% in a single session on the collapse of the ceasefire, with Hormuz still shut. The energy legs did their job (ERX +3.78% on the day) and the diversifiers ate the gains: AAPL -0.56%, XLV -0.61%, RTX -1.52%. So I am cutting the three legs that are no longer earning their weight and putting the capital into the two I actually believe in.

    CUT AAPL (7% to 0). It was bought as a hedge against the tech unwind reversing. It has stopped being that hedge: XLK fell 6.81% in July while AAPL made an all-time high and crossed $5trn. It has decoupled, so it will not protect me if semis keep unwinding, and it is not correlated to anything I need if energy works. On top of that it is a binary print tonight, at an all-time high, into a consensus price target 5% BELOW spot. That is a coin flip I am not paid to take.

    CUT RTX (7% to 0). This is the cleanest sell signal in the packet. RTX beat by 14% and RAISED full-year guidance on 23 July, and then fell — including -1.52% on the day crude gapped 6% on fresh Middle East strikes. A defence name that will not rally on a beat-and-raise INTO a widening war is fully priced. The 'coherent with the supply-shock regime' argument is true and irrelevant if the market refuses to pay for it.

    CUT XLF (11% to 0). It was the one leg with no thesis of its own — its stated job was to supply positive SPY beta so the book was not a pure short-market expression. I am scored on flat dollars, not tracking error, so paying 11 points for beta cosmetics is a waste. It is also the least coherent leg with the mandate: an oil shock at $89 Brent is stagflationary, and the NIM benefit from rising long yields is offset by the credit cost of a squeezed consumer.

    ADD ERX 22% to 32% (64% effective XLE). The single best piece of information I found is that XLE rose 1.88% on a 6.2% crude day. The equity market is pricing this as temporary and crude as mean-reverting; Hormuz has been shut since March and the ceasefire has already failed once. That skepticism is simultaneously my upside (equities have to converge) and my downside cushion (they cannot give back a move they never made — 2026 downside capture on crude down-days was 0.27x). ERX again realised exactly 2.0x with no decay, so I am getting the leverage cleanly. Stop stays at -30%, which caps this leg at 9.6% of NAV and corresponds to roughly a -15% XLE break.

    ADD MPC 9% to 16%. Highest-conviction single name and the only near-dated catalyst I own: 4 August, consensus EPS +184-199% y/y on record cracks, with management having pulled 40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 specifically to run at 94% utilisation into this window. The sell-side average PT of $301.59 is stale and sits below spot while the two most recent revisions are Goldman $376 and TD Cowen $357. Crack spreads are a genuinely different driver from crude beta (-0.16 correlation to SPY), so this is not just more ERX. I am sizing it BEFORE the print because the print is the reason. The -25% stop caps the leg at 4.0% of NAV, which is the price of admission for a stock up 71% YTD.

    ADD XLY SHORT 13% to 17%. The purest expression of the whole thesis and now doing double duty: $89 Brent is a consumer tax, and 39% of this ETF is AMZN plus TSLA — the two names carrying both the consumer squeeze and the AI-valuation de-rating that took XLK down 6.81% in July. At -0.38 correlation to XLE it is additive to the energy core rather than an offset, and it is my only real protection if the market breaks broadly. An ETF, so no single-name squeeze risk; 3% borrow; stop stays -18%.

    HOLD XLV at 20%. This is what lets me carry an 80% effective energy position. -0.07 correlation to XLE, 13.7% vol, +25% over one year, and State Street just moved healthcare to positive for Q3 on pipeline wins. Still unlevered on purpose — I do not want leverage on the ballast.

    HOLD DOGE short 3% at 3x. Unchanged logic and still free leverage: short perps pay zero funding while longs pay leverage x 10% APR. DOGE is at $0.0702, has not participated in any crypto bounce, and the loss is hard-capped at the 3% margin. Trimmed a point to fund the core.

    RISK FRAME. Effective energy exposure goes from ~53% to 80% of NAV. That is the mandate, executed at the size the new rules permit and the news now justifies. The single risk that kills this book is a durable ceasefire headline, because it hits ERX, MPC and the XLY short simultaneously. I have sized so that scenario is survivable rather than hedged away: with both stops firing the arithmetic bound is roughly -13 to -14% of NAV, against an upside of similar magnitude on a 15% XLE convergence — and I take that as skewed in my favour because energy equities never priced the spike they would have to give back. I am keeping 12% in cash at 4% as genuine dry powder rather than forcing it into the same trade; concentration where I have conviction, cash where I do not, and no third-best ideas in between. Filling on the next trading date — crude has already gapped and the equities have not followed, so I do not want to wait.

On top of that it is a binary print tonight, at an all-time high, into a consensus price target 5% BELOW spot. That is a coin flip I am not paid to take.

    CUT RTX (7% to 0). This is the cleanest sell signal in the packet. RTX beat by 14% and RAISED full-year guidance on 23 July, and then fell — including -1.52% on the day crude gapped 6% on fresh Middle East strikes. A defence name that will not rally on a beat-and-raise INTO a widening war is fully priced. The 'coherent with the supply-shock regime' argument is true and irrelevant if the market refuses to pay for it.

    CUT XLF (11% to 0). It was the one leg with no thesis of its own — its stated job was to supply positive SPY beta so the book was not a pure short-market expression. I am scored on flat dollars, not tracking error, so paying 11 points for beta cosmetics is a waste. It is also the least coherent leg with the mandate: an oil shock at $89 Brent is stagflationary, and the NIM benefit from rising long yields is offset by the credit cost of a squeezed consumer.

    ADD ERX 22% to 32% (64% effective XLE). The single best piece of information I found is that XLE rose 1.88% on a 6.2% crude day. The equity market is pricing this as temporary and crude as mean-reverting; Hormuz has been shut since March and the ceasefire has already failed once. That skepticism is simultaneously my upside (equities have to converge) and my downside cushion (they cannot give back a move they never made — 2026 downside capture on crude down-days was 0.27x). ERX again realised exactly 2.0x with no decay, so I am getting the leverage cleanly. Stop stays at -30%, which caps this leg at 9.6% of NAV and corresponds to roughly a -15% XLE break.

    ADD MPC 9% to 16%. Highest-conviction single name and the only near-dated catalyst I own: 4 August, consensus EPS +184-199% y/y on record cracks, with management having pulled 40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 specifically to run at 94% utilisation into this window. The sell-side average PT of $301.59 is stale and sits below spot while the two most recent revisions are Goldman $376 and TD Cowen $357. Crack spreads are a genuinely different driver from crude beta (-0.16 correlation to SPY), so this is not just more ERX. I am sizing it BEFORE the print because the print is the reason. The -25% stop caps the leg at 4.0% of NAV, which is the price of admission for a stock up 71% YTD.

    ADD XLY SHORT 13% to 17%. The purest expression of the whole thesis and now doing double duty: $89 Brent is a consumer tax, and 39% of this ETF is AMZN plus TSLA — the two names carrying both the consumer squeeze and the AI-valuation de-rating that took XLK down 6.81% in July. At -0.38 correlation to XLE it is additive to the energy core rather than an offset, and it is my only real protection if the market breaks broadly. An ETF, so no single-name squeeze risk; 3% borrow; stop stays -18%.

    HOLD XLV at 20%. This is what lets me carry an 80% effective energy position. -0.07 correlation to XLE, 13.7% vol, +25% over one year, and State Street just moved healthcare to positive for Q3 on pipeline wins. Still unlevered on purpose — I do not want leverage on the ballast.

    HOLD DOGE short 3% at 3x. Unchanged logic and still free leverage: short perps pay zero funding while longs pay leverage x 10% APR. DOGE is at $0.0702, has not participated in any crypto bounce, and the loss is hard-capped at the 3% margin. Trimmed a point to fund the core.

    RISK FRAME. Effective energy exposure goes from ~53% to 80% of NAV. That is the mandate, executed at the size the new rules permit and the news now justifies. The single risk that kills this book is a durable ceasefire headline, because it hits ERX, MPC and the XLY short simultaneously. I have sized so that scenario is survivable rather than hedged away: with both stops firing the arithmetic bound is roughly -13 to -14% of NAV, against an upside of similar magnitude on a 15% XLE convergence — and I take that as skewed in my favour because energy equities never priced the spike they would have to give back. I am keeping 12% in cash at 4% as genuine dry powder rather than forcing it into the same trade; concentration where I have conviction, cash where I do not, and no third-best ideas in between. Filling on the next trading date — crude has already gapped and the equities have not followed, so I do not want to wait.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: One leg of this book was built on reasoning that facts falsified within 24 hours of my writing it, and correcting a wrong thesis is not churn. I wrote that 39% of XLY sat at the intersection of the consumer squeeze and the AI de-rating. Both halves are now false: AMZN posted accelerating 37% AWS growth and rose 15.6% on 7/31, so 23% of my biggest short is an AI winner; TSLA is another 16% and expensive gasoline is a tailwind for EVs, meaning I was short a beneficiary inside an oil-tax trade. And the oil tax itself is easing at the pump — gasoline peaked above $5.00 in mid-June and is now ~$4.27, with ex-gasoline retail spending resilient. That leg has to go, and I am not paying to keep a short whose largest holdings are structurally on the wrong side of my own thesis. I am replacing it with the same trade expressed correctly. Airlines are the direct P&L counterparty to my refiner long: refiners earn the record crack, airlines pay it, jet fuel is +130% y/y at up to a quarter of opex, Spirit is already gone and the $2.5bn budget-carrier bailout has been publicly rejected by the administration — yet JETS trades near the top of its 52-week range. Second change: the evidence for refining margins hardened materially while the evidence for crude-beta convergence did not. Valero reported after I set this book, beat by 27%, and guided Q3 capture rates ABOVE Q2 on cheaper feedstock, against an all-time-high 3-2-1 crack. That driver is refinery capacity shortage, not Hormuz, so it partly survives the ceasefire headline that is the single scenario that kills this book, whereas 2x crude beta does not. So I move six points out of ERX into VLO and keep the energy weight roughly where it was while shifting its centre of gravity from the leg I merely believe to the leg that is confirmed. Everything I got right stays untouched: ERX, XLV, MPC and the DOGE perp keep their sizes and stops, and I pay no cost on them. Cash rises to 17% deliberately — not indecision but the only real hedge against a durable ceasefire, held at 4% with MPC printing Tuesday as a live reason to deploy it.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: I am exiting refining entirely because the thesis was falsified by the people who run the companies. I sized MPC at 16% on the specific premise that management front-loaded ~40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 to run flat-out into this window, and I added VLO at 10% because its CEO had guided Q3 margins above Q2 with the binary print already behind it. On the 4 August call MPC told me Q3 carries ~$290mn of turnaround expense plus planned conversion-unit maintenance, that Q3 historically averages 95% capture against the 112% just printed, that early-Q3 margins are 'not at Q2 levels', that the jet-to-diesel spread has narrowed and that some Q2 drivers were 'not repeatable'. That is my sizing premise reversed by the issuer. The tape says the same thing louder: a 27% EPS beat ($17.73 vs $13.95, $5.1bn net income, margin doubled to $36.33/bbl) and the stock closed 8/7 at $301, below the ~$314 where I bought it. When a print that good cannot lift a stock, the forward money has already left. The commodity confirms it — the 3-2-1 crack's all-time $70-72 was a July peak, NY Harbor diesel has fallen from 84c on 10 July to ~60c and is now below its five-year average, distillate exports set an all-time weekly record, and EIA looks for significantly narrower cracks in 4Q26. Holding a token position with a dead thesis is worse than holding none, so both go. Second, Friday's payrolls print (-23k vs +80k, with ~100k of downward revisions to May and June, wage growth at a 2021 low) is a genuine regime break: an oil-driven inflation impulse landing on a contracting labor market. That is demand-negative for exactly the refined products I just sold, and it re-prices the Fed from a possible hike to cuts. The asset that wins in both tails of my own book is precious metals — it gets the haven bid if Hormuz escalates and the rate-cut bid if the strait reopens into a weakening economy — so gold becomes my largest single position at 20% with silver at 7% for beta to the same call. I take this in bullion, not miners: GDX/GDXJ have been squeezing shorts violently, which tells me the direction is right and the entry is extended, and I do not need levered operating gearing stacked on top of a 2x energy fund. Third, I keep the energy core because it is the one leg the week actually confirmed — crude fell ~5% and XLE gave up only ~1.5%, XLE rose 1.48% on Friday against a down tape, and energy is still the best-performing US sector. But 26% of a 2x fund is a 52% effective single-sector bet, and the de-escalation path is no longer a headline, it is a draft accord sitting in the Iranian parliament. Trimming to 20% keeps 40% effective XLE as my largest risk exposure while the labor data resolves. XLV goes up rather than down because the defensive rotation is now the trade and not merely the ballast — it closed 8/7 at $165.68 near a 52w high of $168.53, +29% on the year, 0.56 beta, and it is explicitly being bought as the haven for money leaving tech. JETS comes down to 6%: the demand half of the short improved on Friday but the cost half is going the wrong way, and I have the June precedent that a fuel-price drop puts 6-7% into airline stocks in one session. It is a labor-rollover short now, not a fuel-cost short, and it is smaller because it stays directionally additive to whatever energy exposure I still carry. Total turnover is roughly 65% one-way at ~2bps a side, about 1.3bps of NAV — cheap enough that being wrong for another week costs far more than the trade does.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: I cut energy from 26% to 20% last week for one stated reason: an Iran-Oman draft accord sitting in the Iranian parliament made the de-escalation binary too live to run a 52% effective single-sector bet into. That reason weakened this week rather than strengthened. The accord is deadlocked, Iran has re-anchored on ending the war and sanctions relief as preconditions, the US has committed to an indefinite blockade, ship attacks continued, and Hormuz vessel traffic fell rather than normalised. At the same time the physical case got materially better: the IEA doubled its Q3 deficit to 1.8 mb/d, the deepest since Q4 2021, which draws barrels regardless of what any parliament does. And the reason I thought I had spent my cushion — XLE +6% on the week — does not survive the wider frame: Brent printed above $120 earlier this year on this same closure and sits at $88.52 today. The premium has been faded, not extended. So energy goes back up. The second change follows from the same fact: JETS is the only leg where both drivers turned my way in the same week, cost and demand, and it is simultaneously my only hedge against an S&P sitting at a record. I am funding both out of a 19% cash pile that was insurance against a resolution the week made less likely. The rest of the book is untouched in size — I am tightening stops on three legs that have run, because on a 2x fund and on metals up 10% in a month, size is the real protection and the stop only bounds what is left.

WHAT IS DRIVING IT: FOMC on 29-Jul plus "chip worries spread." That is the textbook falling-implied-correlation regime my mandate is built on, and it is now confirmed violently rather than merely inferred. Even grossing the decay up for the fact that QQQ realized vol is running at the 80th percentile (decay scales with sigma-squared, so maybe 2x the historical mean) it only gets to roughly break-even, against a backtested worst 63-day of -27.76% of notional. That is variance with no expected return, so the leg gets cut hard rather than upsized — which is the opposite of what "high vol in the tech complex" naively suggested.

StrategyClassified the current tape as a calm-index / high-dispersion regime (SPY 20d realized vol 11.65%, 34th percentile of two years, 10d/60d term ratio 0.80, versus QQQ 23.66% and XLK 30.67% at the ~80th percentile, and an implied-correlation proxy that has fallen from 0.54 to 0.34), and sized the book to that state: 60% in vol-targeted low-vol equity (USMV, SPLV) rather than the high-vol tech complex, 12% in SVXY to harvest the ~7-point gap between VIX 18.6 and SPY realized 11.65, a delta-neutral short-gamma pair of equal short TQQQ and short SQQQ to collect leveraged-ETF compounding decay, and 5% VIXY as convex crash insurance with a take-profit that monetises a spike.

Novelty statementI run no Round-2 book, so there is no overlap to manage; the novelty against my own prior book is that I have replaced a paid-for-defensiveness structure (min-vol and low-vol funds that buy calm with surrendered return, plus a front-month vol ETF paying ~50%/yr to carry) with an earned-defensiveness structure - equal-weight index beta that gets its low volatility free from record dispersion, and an energy leg that has historically been positive on the days the index falls hardest - cutting the bleeding hedge to true tail size rather than treating insurance as a position.

RSP realizes 9.79% at 20d and 10.92% at 60d against SPY's 13.33% and 13.93%: the equal-weighted index collects roughly a quarter less volatility from exactly the dispersion I identified, because SPY's ~40% megacap concentration in names realizing 25-45% (QQQ 23.64, XLK 32.73, SMH 46.39) claws most of the correlation benefit back. Same return, less volatility, less drawdown, better crash behaviour, at 20d, 60d and 1y. This is what a high-dispersion regime is supposed to pay a long-only book, and I was leaving it on the table. Measuring it now: VIXM/VIXY rose +3.9% over five sessions against a ~1.1%/week average across the prior three months, and after netting each fund's beta to spot (VIXY ~0.87, VIXM ~0.45) that leaves roughly a point a week of excess front-month decay, about 50% annualised. The carry advantage I paid up for has not merely faded, it has inverted, and the leg is -9.4% on the month as a result. The value case thinned in parallel and not in the way I expected: VIX at 14.25 against 10d realized of 11.64% is 2.6 points of premium - near a normal risk premium, not a cheap one - and it got there because realized vol fell faster than implied, with 10d 11.64 below 20d 13.33 below 60d 13.93. I am cutting rather than exiting because the reasons to hold insurance are still genuinely present and cheap on the axes that matter for convexity: VVIX at 87.48 means options on VIX itself are near the low end of their range, SKEW rose 4.4% to 138.36 during a week ATM vol fell 4.4% so someone is quietly bidding tails, VIX sits at the 2nd percentile of its trailing year, and the 15-16 September FOMC is a dated binary inside my horizon now carrying an active energy-inflation impulse. This leg was positive by +5.8% to +12.4% on every one of SPY's eight worst days of the year; nothing else I own is convex like that. So it stays, at a size that is honestly a tail hedge rather than a position, funded partly into XLE which expresses the same shock at positive carry. Take-profit held at +60% so a moderate scare leaves the hedge intact and only a genuine dislocation converts it to cash. No stop, for the reason that has never changed: stopping out of insurance while it is losing money is the one thing insurance must never be allowed to do.

  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_volregime.json

    Outlook at registrationI expect a low-volatility, positively-skewed-in-stress return profile: roughly 8-9% annualized portfolio vol against SPY's 11.65% realized, grinding out carry from the variance premium and the leveraged-ETF decay while the low-vol equity core supplies muted beta. In a continued calm melt-up this book should make money but lag SPY by several points a quarter; in a correlation spike it should be roughly flat to positive while SPY falls, because VIXY's convexity and the short-TQQQ leg both pay. Management at the weekly reassessment is explicitly regime-driven and mechanical: if SPY 20d realized vol rises through roughly 18% or the 10d/60d ratio moves above 1.3, I cut SVXY toward zero, cut the short-gamma pair (trend is its enemy), raise VIXY and cash, and rotate the equity core further toward USMV; if realized vol falls back under 10% with VIX still near 18 I add to SVXY and the decay pair. If dispersion compresses — the implied-correlation proxy climbing back toward 0.55 — the case for holding low-vol equity over the index weakens and I would move the core toward broader beta. The specific thing that would make me abandon the construction is realized vol printing above implied for several weeks, which would mean the premium I am being paid has gone negative.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31; 2025-02-14 to 2025-05-30 (stress)

    Numbers are verbatim from `python3 tracker/round2.py --backtest <entry> <end> <file>` on this exact construction. The engine reports NAV $1041.42 / $1016.88 / $1054.73 on $1000. THE CENTRAL CAVEAT: a static allocation cannot switch regimes mid-window, which is the entire point of the strategy. These three windows therefore test whether the CURRENT regime call (calm index, high dispersion, wide variance premium) would have survived three different historical tapes — they do NOT test the switching rule, which only becomes visible across weekly reassessments in the live round. The book underperforms SPY by 4.6 and 8.2 points in the two rising windows and beats it by 8.5 points in the stress window; that asymmetry is the intended character, not a defect, but it means a sustained melt-up is the most likely way this book finishes behind. STOP DESIGN, FOUND BY ITERATION: an earlier candidate carried 30% stops on both leveraged-ETF legs and returned -5.92% with a -11.20% drawdown in 2026H1, because a whipsaw stopped out first one leg and then the other, twice converting a hedged pair into a naked directional short; removing the per-leg stops took the same window to +1.62% and the stress window from -0.05% to +7.83%. The pair is therefore risk-controlled by SIZE and by the natural floor on a short, not by stops. SVXY's stop was likewise widened from 18% to 25% after the tighter level fired at the March-2026 vol bump and locked in a loss the position then recovered. SHORT-VOL TAIL RISK, STATED PLAINLY: the accepted loss on a 1-day -21% / 5-day -34% SVXY event is about -3 to -4% of NAV after the stop, partly offset by VIXY, and the engine only checks stops at daily closes, so an intraday gap would fill worse than the stop level. In the stress window SVXY hit its stop and VIXY hit its take-profit (the engine prints these closures as LIQUIDATED) and the book still finished +5.47%, which is the hedge working as designed. Other caveats: no market impact or borrow-availability constraint on the leveraged-ETF shorts, flat 3% borrow and 10% funding, and daily-close granularity throughout.

  3. 2026-08-03REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus5_volregime.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus5_volregime.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I am not touching the equity core, which is a session old and needs no change; I am closing the two carry legs because one had its premise refuted overnight and the other was already refuted by my own arithmetic. SVXY existed to harvest the gap between implied and realized index vol. When I sized it that gap was ~7 points; after VIX collapsed 22% to ~16 against SPY realized of ~13-14% it is ~2-3 points. Getting paid 2-3 points to be short the tail is thin at the best of times, and this is not the best of times: the 10y just broke to 4.75% on $100 oil and an escalating Middle East conflict, which is precisely the macro shock that drags implied correlation back up and hurts a short-index-vol position most. The carry shrank and the tail fattened simultaneously, so the leg goes. The TQQQ/SQQQ pair is me correcting a documented mistake rather than reacting to news: on 7/30 I wrote that my own backtest gives it ~1.2%/yr on notional against 3% APR borrow on EACH leg — roughly -0.25% of NAV per year with a -27.76% worst 63-day — and then kept it at 7+7 anyway because it 'expressed the regime.' That was attachment to a narrative over my own numbers. It is a negative-carry structure whose best environment is chop and whose worst is trend, and an oil-and-rates shock is a trending catalyst, so the case only got weaker. Closing both costs about 26% turnover at ~2-2.5bps, roughly $0.07, and it is economically positive from day one: I stop paying 0.42%/yr of NAV in borrow and start earning 4% on the cash. VIXY goes up rather than down as the exact mirror of my 7/30 trim — I cut it then because buying insurance at VIX 20.66 right after a pop is paying up post-event, and the same insurance now costs ~22% less in VIX terms while the event it insures against became materially more likely. Buy convexity when it is cheap and the tail is fat; that is the discipline, and it is the reason I can still run an 78% low-vol equity core. The 16% cash is deliberate, not a residual: with my short-vol carry removed and a live geopolitical/inflation catalyst, dry powder that pays 4% is the right way to hold risk in reserve, and it funds adding to the core if the rate shock hands me a better entry. Net result is a simpler book, lower gross, no borrow, more cash yield, and my two best-evidenced legs plus a cheap hedge.

  4. 2026-08-10REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_volregime.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_volregime.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Two things moved enough to force this, and they point the same way. First, the volatility risk premium has closed: VIX 15.15 against SPY 20d realized 13.49% is ~1.7 points, versus a ~3-4 point norm, so index vol is no longer expensive - and Cboe implied correlation sits at a 23-year low (COR3M ~9-10, 52-week range 9.29-11.95), which is a bounded, mean-reverting quantity that can only normalise upward. Long index vol therefore pays if realized rises OR correlation normalises, and the compressed contango (VX6/VX1 1.062 vs a 1.15-1.20 norm) means I pay a third-to-half the carry I underwrote at entry. Cheaper insurance against a denser calendar - CPI 12-Aug, a stalled Hormuz fee dispute with Brent at $80, and a 15-16 Sep FOMC where a Warsh hike is still 44% priced after payrolls printed -23k with 103k of downward revisions. Second, and this is the correction I owe myself: I have been conflating vol targeting with owning low-vol stocks. Vol targeting scales exposure to the INDEX by the index's realized vol. USMV and SPLV buy their low vol by surrendering expected return and by parking 25% of SPLV in utilities ahead of a live hike; the index buys its low vol from diversification, which is free and is at a 23-year maximum precisely because correlation is at a 23-year low. At COR3M ~10 the S&P realizes 13.5% while its average constituent realizes far more - that makes SPY the cheapest carrier of equity risk in my universe right now, not USMV. My book was carrying only ~40 SPY-equivalent betas into a low-correlation, low-index-vol tape and made +0.97% while the index made +3.58% and tech made +7.2%. The fix is not to abandon defence, it is to take the permission the insurance already bought: raise index beta and raise the hedge together. Modelled across three states - calm melt-up, moderate scare, and a VIX-doubling shock - the new shape beats the old one in every one, because more cheap convexity is what makes more beta affordable rather than a substitute for it.

  5. 2026-08-17REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-17/opus5_volregime.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-17/opus5_volregime.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Two pieces of my own evidence turned against last week's construction and one turned against last week's arithmetic, so this is a correction rather than a view change - the regime call (calm index, violent components) is unchanged and this book expresses it better.

    First, the arithmetic. I built a 40% SPY core on 'index variance equals average constituent variance times correlation', arguing the cap-weighted wrapper is safer than its contents at a 23-year correlation low. That identity is an equal-weight identity. RSP realizes 9.79% at 20d and 10.92% at 60d against SPY's 13.33% and 13.93%, on the same tape in the same window - the equal-weighted index captures the diversification benefit I was describing while SPY's megacap concentration consumes most of it. I checked this was not a 20-day artefact before acting on it: over the trailing year RSP returned +21.8% against SPY's +22.0% with a smaller max drawdown (-7.9% vs -8.9%) and roughly 68% average downside capture across SPY's eight worst days. Identical return, a quarter less volatility, at all three horizons. If my mandate is return per unit of realized vol, RSP is simply the better vehicle for the exact thesis I already hold, so 30% moves to RSP and SPY keeps 20% because I am correcting an expression, not abandoning cap-weighted beta entirely.

    Second, the carry. VIXM/VIXY moved +3.9% in five sessions against a ~1.1%/week three-month average; netting each ETF's beta to spot leaves roughly a point a week of excess front-month decay, about 50% annualised. On 08-08 I explicitly justified upsizing VIXY to 11% on the claim that compressed contango had cut my roll cost to a third-to-a-half of the 43.8%/yr underwritten at entry. That claim is now false by my own measurement. Separately, the value case has thinned: VIX 14.25 against 10d realized 11.64% is 2.6 points of premium, near normal, and realized is falling faster than implied. I am not abandoning the hedge - VVIX at 87 is cheap convexity, SKEW rose to 138 in a week VIX fell, and the 15-16 Sep FOMC is a dated live binary inside my horizon - but a leg whose price of carry has doubled while its value case thinned should shrink to true insurance size, so 11% goes to 7% with the take-profit untouched.

    Third, SPLV. I kept it for tech-free diversification, but its protection is a rates bet and rates went the wrong way: ^TNX to 4.70 with ^IRX pinned at 3.70, a long-end-led steepening, which is precisely the inflation-expectations move an +7.9% Brent week produces. XLU -2.55% and SPLV -0.57% on the month confirm it. Once RSP is in the book, SPLV's broad-diversification role is redundant and only its concentrated utilities bet remains, so I exit it.

    What replaces it is the reason I am comfortable cutting the vol sleeve. XLE printed positive on five of SPY's eight worst days of the trailing year - better crash behaviour than SPLV's four of eight - while returning +49.2% over that year against SPLV's +6.2%. It is long the one macro shock actually running (Brent +7.9%, XLE +7.7%, USO +7.3% in a week the S&P gained 0.4% and VIX fell), and an energy-led inflation impulse is the single state where SPY, USMV and cash all lose together and only my hedges help. Sized at just 7% because it realizes 24.5% vol and because a leg that ran 7.7% in five sessions deserves respect, not enthusiasm. The net effect is a book with the same equity beta, materially less realized volatility, a hedge that earns rather than bleeds, and 18% cash at 4% into a live September Fed.
